And, of course, the hon-gentleman will have the information we ask for before he brings the item up again. That is only reasonable.
Before we leave this item, I would call the attention of the government to some evidence given by Mr. Charles M. Hays before Judge Winchester. The report is as follows :

Hays, second vice-president and general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway system, examined by Mr. Mowat, testified that on June 16, 1903, he wrote to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, informing him that the Grand Trunk Pacific had nine surveying parties in the field, and of nine locating engineers, four were Canadians, three Americans, one was a German arid one an Englishman.
I do not know whether there is any mistake in the date-16th June, 1903. I have not observed that that letter has been brought down. Further he says :
When witness, in reply to a communication from Hon. Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance, wrote that of the thirteen engineers employed on the work, but three were Americans, the other being British subjects, he relied upon Mr. Stephens for the information.
Possibly that letter may have been brought down. I have sent for a copy of the correspondence, which I have not yet had an opportunity of examining very carefully. There is no date given, and one would have to look over the entire correspondence to see if this letter is included. But if these letters or any others relating to the matter have not been brought down, I think they should be brought down a once.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) give me the dates S

Yes, and I will also give the reference to the report. The date given by Mr. Hays for the letter he wrote to the Prime Minister is 16th June, 1963. The date of the letter to Mr. Fielding is not given. The report from which I quote is that contained in the Montreal 1 Gazette ' of July 5th.	[DOT]

There is another matter in connection with these surveys. I would like, as far as possible, to have -what information the government may have in re-

gard to the grades and curvatures on the surveys that have already been made. The House will remember that last session a gentleman very close to the government made the statement to the House that the surveys between Winnipeg and Lake Nipigon had shown that they were able to get grades and curvatures such as they stated would be essential tor the road as they propose to build it-grades of some twenty feet to the mile and curvatures of some three or four degrees. I would be glad if the minister would prepare to tell us some-j thing in regard to that matter, because it ig very important to the people of the district from which I come.
Railways and canals-chargeable to capital -canals-Cornwall canal, enlargement, $26,500.

This is to continue certain work that was commenced in 1902. Of this amount $8,450 is a revote. The amounts to be expended, are as follows:-Repairs and enlargement of regulating weir at old lock 17, $15,500-
Is that at the head of the canal ?

At the lower end of the canal. Protection to north bank, $3,000; Sheik's Island dam, final estimate, $8,000, total, $26,500. The total expenditure on this work up to the 1st May, 1904, was $7,016,.328.33.

It is upon this item that we propose to have the discussion of the so-called Davis contract and the report of the Auditor General. I was informed by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) privately on Wednesday last that he did not desire us to take up this matter in the absence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick). If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Em-merson) is prepared to go on, of course it does not make any difference to us.
If this is the particular item on which the discussion is to take place and the discussion has been arranged for. It was understood on this side that the discussion would take place next Wednesday.

Then, I suppose it would be better to let the item stand.
Mr. EMMBRSOp. Yes, if this is the item to which that .matter relates.
It is. But there is no objection to going into the item so far as other matters are concerned, so long as we have an understanding that the other discussion will not be closed out.
I understand that the arrangement was made that the discussion of that subject will take place next Wednesday.

That is as I understood it, but I wanted to let the hon. minister know that we were ready to go on if the arrangement is varied.
iMr. HAGGART. I understood the hon. minister (Mr. Emmerson) to say that on Wednesday next we would take up the Intercolonial.
That is for Wednesday afternoon, but this other question will come up on Wednesday morning.
You cannot get through in a morning.
We will try. Perhaps we can, if the hon. gentlemen do- not make very long speeches.
There may he half a dozen who will want to make long speeches.
Then we will have to adjourn the debate.

Perhaps you had better make no arrangement about the Intercolonial. If you are going to take the M. P. Davis matter up on Wednesday for lighting the Cornwall canal, that will likely take most of the day.
I said Wednesday, because I expect to be away on Tuesday evening.
The Minister of Justice is here, perhaps he could take up the Davis matter now.

No. Some hon. gentlemen on the other side came to me yesterday and wanted a day fixed after Tuesday. The Minister of Justice says he is ready to go on, but some hon. gentlemen opposite who wanted to go away, asked that the matter be not taken up during their absence.
That is all right. Galops canal-enlargement, $204,300.
Will the minister kindly explain the item ?

This estimate is made up as follows : Under contract: the Iroquois section, $6,300 ; Cornwall section, $88,000 ; Upper entrance, $100,000 ; Iroquois section at Presqu'Ue, $10,000. The above amounts will complete the three sections. For construction purposes, the canal was divided into four sections.
Is there any new work going on now or is this work merely to settle up the whole matter ?
There is a little work going one, but this is the final estimate for that section.

I understood last year that the work was all completed, and that only the final estimates remained to be

made up. Since that time there has been no appearance of much work going on. What are they doing now ?
Mi-. EMMERSON. There is very little work going on, and there is but little work to be done. This amount is to meet the final estimates. The engineers are preparing the final estimates, and this is to pay the contractors.
How many employees are there now on the engineering staff ?
Four or five.
The work was done a year ago, and the minister says there is no work going on now.
They are engaged in making up the final estimates.
I would like to know the number of men that are employed on the engineering staff. They have been doing nothing for the last year, but merely drawing their pay.
If my hon. friend wants that information, I will send over to the department and get it.

Exactly, and we will know who the men are, because, as I understand, they are there, and there is nothing whatever for them to do. Moreover, during the whole of the winter months these men are kept on the pay-list, while in years gone by, when winter came on and work closed on these contracts, all these men that were employed at that work were let go. But since the hon. gentleman has been carrying on this work these men have been kept on during the whole winter, not only during the whole winter but since the work has been completed. I would like to know how much longer they are going to be kept there.
During the winter months, as I understand from the deputy, they were all off excepting the engineers, and subsequently two men were employed doing certain work with the engineers.
Then they were off during the winter. I find in the Auditor General's Report, one man, Wm. Matthews, timber inspector, 12 months, $960.
The hon. gentleman is referring to 1903 is he not ?
I know this man was on part of this last winter at all events.
I said a part of the winter.
I would like to know the names of the men that are on now, and in the meantime we could let the item stand till we get that information.
I will get the information, but I do not think that we should let the item stand.

It has been understood that the work has been completed for over a year. You have the staff there permanently' the whole year round. The inspector of masonry is now on the work drawing bis salary' notwithstanding the fact that the work has been done for two years.
The amount expended on the Cardinal section since the 1st of July last year and up to the first of May of the present year is $19,060.
If the hon. gentleman could give the names of the men who are employed, I would be able to judge what it is costing to keep these men there when there is no work going on.

The hon. gentleman states there is no work going on. The deputy tells me there has been work going on. The work has been continued. There is still some work to do and in so far as the engineers are concerned they are still at work in connection with the final estimate.

There is no question about the engineers being employed as yet. There should be work for them to do in getting up the final estimate, but the masonry has been done for two years and I understand the inspector of masonry Mr. Connley, who is down in the Auditor General's Report for his pay for 12 months up to the 1st July last year is still on. After the work has been completed why is it this inspector is being kept on ? A few days after I brought this matter up last year they let these men go, but a meeting was held and it was decided to put them all on again after the House had risen. They were immediately put on and they are still on. I would like to know what they are doing ?
You are asking for $204,300. Does that complete the work ?
Yes', that completes the three sections.
These are not the same sections for which this $25,000 was voted last year ?
Yes, these are the same sections.

In 1903-4 we had in the estimates $253,000. That was for a specific section. In the same column this year we are asked for $204,300. I would assume that $204,300 is for the same work that we voted the $253,000 for last year ? Is that right ?

The $204,300 is to cover three sections, the Iroquois, Cardinal and upper entrance and some new work on the Iroquois section consisting of cribwork at Presqu'Ile. That $253,000 voted last year was very largely for the upper entrance.

As far as I can make out the $253,000 voted last year was to complete

the whole work. Now we are asked for $204,300 for the Galops canal enlargement. Last year the vote was :
Galops canal-enlargement, $125,000.
This is to pay the final estimate of Messrs. Larkin & Sangster on their contract for the Iroquois section. The work is completed.
How much has been voted this session for this canal ?	.
There was in the main estimates for the Galops canal an item of $128,000.
Does that include the Iroquois canal ?
No. That item we have now is for the Iroquois canal.
There have been items voted for the Cardinal section. Does this finish the whole work ?

Yes, I am advised that the estimates1 of the current year are expected to cover the whole expense.
I am not very familiar with the matter but it appears to me that that covers the whole work we are discussing now.

When I asked that question last year the minister then in charge informed the committee that the work was completed, that that was the final estimate and that the item of $128,000 was for the whole work on the Cardinal section. Notwithstanding that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals says that there is $88,000 in this estimate which is now before the committee for this same work.

In settling up the final estimate it was found that this $88,000 is necessary to meet the cost of construction.
Mr. .1. D. REID. But, the hon. minister will see the question of last year. I will read it again.
There have been items voted for the Cardinal section. Does this finish the whole work ?

Yes, I am advised that the estimates of the current year are expected to cover the whole expense.
So ' that you will see that that was the final estimate. That was the amount that was put into the estimates prepared by the department and which was intended to wind up the whole work. Now the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals brings down an estimate for $88,000 and makes the saine statement that this is expected to complete the work. This is a part I cannot understand and one in regard to which I would like to have a little further information.
It was estimated last year that the sum asked for would pay the whole cost, hut the work exceeded the estimate and it has been determined by the final estimate that $S8.000 more will be required.
But the work was all completed then.

It was not finally settled. It is of course carried out upon schedule rates. There was a difference as to the quantities and it turns out that $88,000 is still required to settle up what was finally determined as the amount.
The estimates are made up monthly.
The progress estimates are but the final settlement of the matter is not.
Then the minister says that a mistake of $88,000 was made by the engineers in preparing the estimate last year.

No, I did not state that. I stated that they found they still required the $88,000. At that time they were not in a position to definitely settle upon the amount and since that they have engaged in the work of making up these final estimates and have reached that view with respect to them.

The minister does not seem to realize the situation. Surely when there is a mistake of $88,000 there is at least the duty upon the minister and the department to inform parliament of the state of things at the earliest possible moment and too explicitly call the attention of parliament to the mistake. That is not the attitude the minister has taken and he would have allowed this item to go through without giving any information. We should have all the information that was before the department last year and ail the information that was collected since then in reference to this matter in order that we may have an opportunity of criticising this carefully to see that there has been no unlawful leakage and no improper diversion of money. We have had it stated by a member who knows the situation that there does appear to have been a substantial leakage by the engagement of men who should not have -been engaged and the retention of men whose services should not have been retained. He should allow this item to stand in order that he may bring a full statement in writing of the basis upon which the estimate was made last year, and the data collected since then showing how it is and where it is that this discrepancy of $88,000 has arisen.

It would be very difficult to get the evidence of the gentleman who made the estimate. These estimates are furnished in this way. The resident engineer, the superintending engineer, sends in to the department his estimate. That gentleman was Mr, Rubidge.
It was not Mr. Rubidge who made up the estimate ; it was the engineer in charge of the work at Cardinal.
He was the superintending engineer of ail these works and it was he who sent to the department as his own estimate the progress estimates of the contractors at the different points.

Thesq estimates have been prepared for some time; they have been before this House for some months. The minister knows well of course that the late Mr. Rubidge only died about two weeks ago and up to within a week before his death he was as active as he ever was. He therefore sent in his estimate and you have ail the papers of Mr. Rubidge in connection with this.

We have all his estimates ; we have the estimate wherein it was shown that $128,000 or whatever was asked last year was sufficient to complete the work. We also have the further estimate from Mr. Rubidge which appears in these estimates stating that it would require $8S,000 more. That was received before March last because at that time these estimates were made out.
The work is practically done ; there is no doubt about that.
I can neither deny nor confirm that statement, but the deputy of the department tells me that the work is not done. The trimming up work of the canal is not yet done.
The trimming up work ?
That is a very important feature.
When does the minister expect the work will be finally completed ?

The deputy is hurrying up the officials in every possible way, urging them to have the work completed. The department is doing their very best in that direction and are anxious to have the final estimates as to the work.
It was reported to me a few days ago that there had been another slide of the stone work with which the banks of the canal are faced. What is the position in relation to that ?
Nothing of that kind has been reported to the department.

I have not been there for the last few days. Last year there were three large slides. I would ask the minister if this damage has been repaired and I would also ask if the government did it at their expensive or were the contractors compelled to do that at their own expense ?
The contractors did it; they are supposed to do it at their own expense.
Is there anything in this $88,000 for that or will they be paid for that ?
No, the deputy says that is not included in this.
Will the minister tell us when he got the final estimate for this work ?
I have not the final estimate.	_
I mean of the contractors work for the completion of this canal. Have they not the final estimates yet ?
Of the Iroquois section they have not.
I understood that the final estimate was included in this $88,000.
We have not the final estimate but the deputy says that this amount will certainly cover the item.
The whole work.
That is what the deputy assures me.

Then you are giving me the same answer as l received last year which was :
Yes, I am advised the estimates of the current year are expected to cover the whole expenditure.
And this is the same answer this year. What will the answer be next year ? What is the total amount that has been expended on this up to date.

The total expended on section 1, that is from Iroquois to Pres-qu'Isle, up to the 30th of June, 1902, was $1,277,770 ; from the 30th June, 1902 to the 30th of June, 1903, $12,418.20; total expended up to the 30th of June, 1903, $1,290,188.20 ; total expended up to the 1st of May, 1904, $1,366,856.40. Larkin & Sang-ster are the contractors. On section No. 2, from Presqu'Isle to Gates Point, known as the Cardinal section, on which William Davis & Sons had the contract, the total amount expended to May 1st was $4,108,920. On section 3, from Gates Point to Upper Entrance, known as the Upper Entrance section, on which the contractors are Murray & Cleveland, the total expenditure .to the 1st of May was $1,866,998.15. Section 4, outside Upper Entrance, W. A. Allan, contractor, was completed some years ago. The total expenditure to the 1st of May, 1904, was $5,439,238.24.
Was the payment to Mr. Allan on account of the Galops canal ?
He had section 4 ot the Galops canal.
Has the minister done anything about arranging to have the bridge at Cardinal swung by some other means than hand power ?
That matter is receiving the attention of the department now.
It was receiving it a year ago.
I had the papers under consideration this morning, and some instructions were given with a view to having that work done at once, so that the bridge will be swung by electric power.
If you put on electric power, will the same staff he kept on, or will the number he decreased ?
I think we shall probably not require more than one man in the day and one at night.

This work was finished a couple of years ago. How is it you have not a final estimate, but that you are keeping on a staff of engineers* who have nothing to do but prepare a final estimate ? It is a most extraordinary state of affairs.

The real fact is that such details are required by the Auditor General with respect to the matter that it is impossible to get all these gathered. I presume the late superintending engineer was in the confidence of my hon. friend, and he would not say that he was purposely delaying the work. He was in his lifetime urged to have the work completed, and the department is very anxious indeed to have it completed ; but it has seemed to be impossible to get it done.
Then I am to understand from the hon. gentleman that the staff of the Galops canal is kept on for two years after the work is done for the purpose of furnishing details to the Auditor General ?
The hon. gentleman must not understand that, because that is not what I said.
Those were the exact words the hon. gentleman used.
Excuse me, I did not. My hon. friend said the work was completed two years ago. I stated, on the authority of the deputy minister, that the work is not yet finally completed.
The hon. minister knows that the contractors have left, they have taken their dredges and tugs away, sold their steam shovels, and taken all their plant.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman is speaking from personal knowledge.

I know that their plant is all gone. When the minister says the work is not yet completed, I cannot understand what these people are working at. For instance, why do you require an in-201
spector of masonry, drawing $1,200 a year, when there is not a solitary mason working on the premises ? Surely there must be something wrong in this.
Mr. EMMERSON, My hon. friend must surely be labouring under some mistake. I understand he is speaking of the Iroquois section ?
No, the Cardinal section.

There is some work going on there, the engineer states. There are five men employed, namely, two chain-men, the engineer, the assistant engineer, and the masonry inspector ; but on the Iroquois section there are only the clerks, the engineer and the assistant clerk.
I am speaking particularly of the Cardinal section. Will the hon. gentleman tell me why chainmen are required there when there is no engineer to do the work other than make up the final estimates ?
But there is some work on the Cardinal section which the deputy says is going on. My hon. friend says it is not, and of course I could not act as arbitrator between the two.
Is there any masonry going on ?
My deputy says that work must be going on or the services of the men would not be required.
Is there anything going on in the winter time ?
We employ by the year. It is often cheaper to do that than employ a man only a few months. We want a man to commence as inspector and continue the work, and do not want to be changing every month.
' D. REID. If there is any work going on.
I shall go down there myself and make sure.

I wish the hon. minister would. I am quite satisfied that there are two or three men there who have nothing to do but draw their pay. I would like to know the names of the men of whom the hon. minister has a list, who are employed on the Cardinal section.
They are C. I}. Sargent, F. B. Patterson, M. L. O'Connell, E. Cook and A. Cameron.
The last two are the chainmen and the inspector of masonry, who certainly have nothing to do.

The hon. minister said a while ago that the contracts were not finished. Will he be kind enough to inform me what amount he has paid to either of the



contractors, W. Davis & Co. or Larkin, to the end of July, 1904.
There was expended Dorn the 30th of June 1903 to the 1st of May, 1904, $170,000, of which $19,000 was spent on the Cardinal section up to the 1st of May, 1904.
To whom was that paid 1
To W. Davis & Son.
Was that for work dons during the year ?
Yes.

I would like to draw the minister's attention to what was said two years ago by the then Minister of Railways with respect to this work. When the item for the Galops canal enlargement $293,000, of which $55,000 was a revote, was up, the then Minister of Railways said :
I do not propose to ask parliament tor any money beyond this, part of which is needed to pay the drawbacks. There is an amount of drawbacks which we have to pay out of that $50,000. I do not propose to ask parliament for any more money.
Then he said :
There is nothing in the estimate inserted with any intention of continuing the expenditure on this work. I have concluded not to go on with the work any further.
It must have been a surprise to the minister himself, in view of this statement, to find that large amounts have been expended since then, and the committee will expect that the hon. gentleman will now be able to say when the work will be completed and how much more money will have to be voted for its completion.

I think that the hon. minister hardly understood what I referred to a little while ago. I do not want this item to stand over if that possibly can be avoided, but I hope he will see the justice of placing before the committee later on the estimates upon which the amount of $250,000 last year was based and the supplementary estimates that have since come in. Although the minister says that there is some work still being done, neither he nor his deputy can tell the committee actually what is being done, and the conclusion is irresistible that whether there may be something in the nature of trimming still going on, the contractors are not any longer engaged on the work and that substantially the work was completed more than a year ago. I would call the minister's attention to the undesirability of having this kind of thing prevail. In one aspect of the case it occurs very frequently, and that is, whenever a delay occurs, from whatever cause, it seems to me, looking over the public accounts, the public treasury Mr. HAGGART.
lias to bear the interest for the time of the delay. And if it takes nearly two years to complete these final estimates, the result will be that the contractors will be paid not only the amount of the original estimates, but, probably interest as well. That is not fair to the country. I ask the minister particularly to say that he will, at all events, place the papers before the committee at some future time.
The hon. gentleman, if I understand him, asks for the reports from the chief engineer with respect to these payments
Yes, on which they base their estimates. I ask that these be laid on the table. Am I to undestand that that will be done ?
Yes, we will furnish that.

The minister stated that $19,000 had been paid to W. Davis on the contract for the year ending 30th June, 1904. Was any portion of that paid for the three slides that took place on their work, or was it independent of that ?
It is on their contract, not on the slides.
I understand thar the hon. minister is assured by his department that none of the money paid was paid on the slides that occurred on his work ?
That is what the deputy informs me^that it is simply paid on the work done under contract.
That is not an exact answer. I want to know whether any of the money was paid on the slide, and was that included in the contract-was that considered part of the contract ?
I have told my hon. friend distinctly that nothing was paid on the slides ; it was paid on account of the work under the contract, and the slides did not form part of the contract.
I understand the minister now distinctly.

There is the strangest kind of work in connection with this whole matter. I have listened to explanations of ministers for three years in succession. Practically the minister said three years ago : Give me so much money and we will finish the work, we will discharge the hands and the expenditure will stop. And when we came back two years ago he asked an additional amount. What for? To-finish the same work which he had declared the other vote would finish. And still the same men are kept on the work, though, apparently, they have nothing to do except draw their salaries. The minister tells us : My engineer tells me this ; or: My engineer tells me that. The only conclusion that one

can come to is either that the minister, the engineer, and all the rest of them, are in league to take the money from the country, or else that they do not know what they are doing. Though we have been assured so often that the work would be paid for and completed, here again we have $204,300 asked for the same purpose, of which $88,000 is for the contract. What work is being done ? Who is the contractor ? Is the work going on now ? Has there been a* new contract since last year ? These are things we ought to know. We are voting money belonging to the people, and we ought to have information that will be reliable, that we may judge when we reach finality in this affair.
Carried.
It is not carried by any means. We want information from the minister.
It is the same old contract, anyhow. The work has been done under the original contract by the contractors, whose names I have given.

When was the contract given ?	.
, Mr. EMMERSON. In 1897.
Carried.
It is not carried, Mr. Chairman ; and you need not be in such a hurry. It will not be carried until we get the information we ask for.
My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) need not lose his temper.
I am not losing my temper over the minister, but over the chairman calling ' carried ' even when the minister is on his feet and speaking.
I hope the hon. gentleman will not allow himself to be disturbed even by you, Mr. Chairman. We do so much better when we are all amiable and good-natured.
This is too much of a farce to be good-natured over.
Now I am sorry 1 spoke; I am afraid I make my hon. friend angry. I am anxious to give all the information possible.

Then I ask the hon. minister if he will be good enough to give us the information we ask for : Who is the contractor ? Has any new contract been let since last year ? What is the nature of the work being done ? When is it expected that it will be finished ?
Wm. Davis & Sons have the contract for the Cardinal section of this work. Of course, there are several sections.

We are speaking of the Cardinal section.
2014	.

The contract was entered into in 1897. There has been no new contract, and all payments from 1897 down to the present time in connection with the work were paid under that contract; and the Auditor General, in his approval of the payments, calculated with regard to the original contract.
What work is being done at the present time ?
I am informed that the trimming up work is being done.
What does the hon. minister mean by ' trimming up ' ?
It is a technical term with which I am not familiar.
The hon. gentleman will become familiar with it.

I suppose I shall. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) seems disposed to trim me, and I suppose I shall have to get used to it. The chief engineer and deputy minister tell me that the work now being done on the Cardinal section is the final work, that of trimming up the canal-in other words, putting on the finishing touches.
The hon. gentleman has the engineer at his side, cannot he ask him what ' trimming up ' means ?
It means trimming up the slopes and giving the canal the finishing touches.

I may say that was done a year ago. The work was nicely levelled off and sodded, and the sides of the bank are covered with stonework. The minister says now that $88,000 is not sufficient, and that there will be more money asked for next year because the final estimates have not been made up.

I do not think I said that. I said this work is practically completed except some finishing work, which is rot a serious matter. But the final estimate has not been made up. After consulting with my deputy, I am getting new light. One of these reports which I will bring down will sffiow that in addition to this $88,000, the judgment of the late engineer was that we would require $30,000 more to pay final estimates.
Mr. .1. D. REID. Then I must tell the people there that in addition to this $88,000. at least $30,000 will be required before this
matter is finally settled up.
With sorrow I admit it
Was this contract let on schedule prices, or was it a lump sum?
Schedule prices.
Then are there any extras being allowed on this contract ?
Yes.
I suppose this is an extra. How many years will it be before we may expect these extras will be completed ?

It is always a question as to what is extras. By the term extras, I do not understand those items that are within the bounds of the contract. A man does certain work, and more than was contemplated, but which is provided for under the contract. While it adds to the first estimate of the work, it is not essentially an extra.
Are the contractors doing this trimming ?
Yes, Davis and Sons, on the Cardinal section.

There is another matter I wish to bring up. The effect of placing the canal where the government placed it was virtually to make an island of the village of Cardinal. A bridge had to be put across to allow the people to get into the village, and the effect on the whole, was to injure the property of a great many people in the village on account of the main roatl being cut off. One of these gentlemen was the Rev. George McArthur, whose property was seriously damaged. This gentleman appealed to the government to pay him damages, or to appoint valuators to examine his property and award him some damages. The government refused to send their valuator, and he then employed counsel and asked permission to go before the Exchequer Court. The government granted him that privilege. The case came before the Exchequer Court, and I think it was tried by *Mr. Justice Burbidge, who awarded Mr. McArthur $1,200 damages. The government refused to pay, and appealed to the Supreme Court, and I am told by Mr. McArthur's solicitor that the Supreme Court decided against Mr. McArthur, merely on a technical point, but on account of the injury that was done him they believed that morally his case was good. Still they had to decide against him merely on this technical point, and so this gentleman finds himself without redress. The Supreme Court felt that he was entitled to some redress because they decided that the government should pay all the costs that he had incurred up to and including the Supreme Court. 1 do not know whether the government have decided to pay the costs. At the same time, there are some other persons whose property has been seriously injured in consequence of the canal being placed where it is. I think the government should settle this claim with the Rev. Mr. McArthur and also with others who may apper before the Exchequer Court. J now appeal to the government to settle this claim and give others a chance to appear Mr. SPROULE.
before the Exchequer Court, who consider that they have been injured. Therefore I would like to ask the hon. minister what bis opinion is in so far as this case in concerned ?

I had the circumstances of this case brought recently to my notice. While it excites my sympathy and personal inclination I do not see any reason or any justification for my recommending that the reverend gentleman should be paid. His case does excite my political sympathy, because he is a supporter of a party with which I have been for a lifetime allied, and I would liked to have seen him paid.
You are not as liberal with him as you are with many others.

Yes, if my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) were in a situation like that I would like to see him paid and that.desire would be intensified if his politics were right. The facts of this case, however, are that in the construction of the canal that gentleman and some others were put to some inconvenience. Their lands were not taken from them, their property was not invaded but they were put to some inconvenience, a very remote injury, too remote in the judgment of the Supreme Court to warrant them in having a legal claim. I am afraid my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule), who is a very watch dog of the treasury, would become indignant, if not cross, if we were to pay any claims of that kind. If you pay one you open the door for all similar claims. Any one who thinks he has been injured or put to an inconvenience by a great public work would have a similar claim. The construction of the canal in that place must have been an advantage to the people of that section.
It was a great disadvantage to place the canal where they did in so far as the inhabitants of that village were concerned.
But they would rather have it there than not have the canal.
No, they had the canal' before. It ran around the front end of the village where it did not injure the village at all.
It would be a greater advantage to them to have it larger.
Yes, but it has injured this gentleman's property.

It has not injured his property. It may be a little inconvenient for him and he may have to drive around a little farther. We are all subject to some inconvenience in respect to public utilities. There is hardly a man in Canada but can figure up to some degree an inconvenience that he could value in dollars and cents, but

it is more or less remote. In this case it was very remote.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what the judge of the Exchequer Court thought pf it when he gave judgment in favour of this gentleman.

Other judges seemed to think the judgment of the Exchequer Court was not correct. It is one man against many.
Mr. SPROU'LE. There is another question I would like to ask my hon. friend. He says the reverend gentleman has his sympathy. I would like to know how long he considers he can live on sympathy.
If you will let me have your's for a little while I will tell you how long I can live on it.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if he will agree to this ? The clergyman whose property has heen injured or who has gone through with this case is certainly not in a position financially to appeal it. His property has been very seriously injured. He could not get to-day one-half for it what he could have obtained had the canal been left where it was originally and as his property is encumbered he is not able to appeal the case. The first court decided that he was right, the next that he was wrong. There is yet one final court of appeal and that is the Privy Council in England or parliament here. If parliament will settle the case by giving him a grant, of course that will end it. But if they intend to refuse, now that the Supreme Court have recommended the government to pay the expenses so far, will the government agree to allow this appeal to go to the Privy Council and pay the expenses that may be connected with it ? In case the decision is not in favour of the Reverend Geo. McArthur I am sure he will be satisfied that he probably is not entitled to anything and will abide by the consequences as of course he will be obliged to do.

I have enough difficulty in connection with my own department without invading the jurisdiction of another. When the case went to the Supreme Court it was placed under the control of the Department of Justice. I would not wish to interfere as to that and could not answer my hon. friend's question.

We have the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) here. It is really a very great hardship for this gentleman and the amount of expense incurred by the appeal would be very small. I ask the Prime Minister as a favour to this particular gentleman that he will give him this right to have this case
go to the Privy Council and that the government shall assume the expense in connection with it. I venture to say there is not one hon. gentleman on this side of the House who will object to the cost that may be incurred in taking that case to the Privy Council, and I believe that every hon. gentleman on the other side of the House will take the same view of it. I will not ask that this shall be a precedent in connection with any other claims which shall be brought up. In case there are other claims tried the claimants will have to assume the responsibility of going to the Privy Council themselves, but in this case I ask the right hon. Prime Minister to grant the request.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not giving an opinion in regard to this case but if we are not to adopt the judgment I would rather give it to the reverend clergyman than to the lawyers. It would be less expensive, I am sure.
The right hon. Prime Minister has power to grant that request. If the Prime Minister will stand up and say he will allow it to go he will only be doing justice to tnis gentleman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will ask my colleague the Minister of Justice to look at the claim. Perhaps there may be a moral foundation to the claim, but apparently there is no legal foundation.

The hon. Minister of Justice is here and understands the case thoroughly. I think he can explain anything necessary in connection with it so that this matter can be settled now and this claim can be allowed to go to the Supreme Court.
The hon. Minister of Justice ought to take the view of the Prime Minister that he is entitled to benefit of clergy.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Gourley), although a lawyer, is not aware that benefit of clergy was abolished centuries ago. This case is one of harship undoubtedly but I cannot understand on what principle the government should settle with this reverend gentleman unless we are disposed to settle a multitude of other cases which arise under similar circumstances. This gentleman's property with the property of about twenty others was affected as the result of the construction of this canal, I think it was the right of access to these properties that was injured as a result of the construction of this work. He acted for himself and others.
For himself only.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not sure about that. I have not the facts quite clear in my mind but I think that others were con-

nected with the suit. However, that is not important. A man I think named Kief was also connected with this case. It was decided that if the suppliants succeeded in this case the government would pay all parties interested, and if they failed the result in this case would apply "to all. The claim was made against the Railways and Canals Department, it was referred to my department, and I thought it my duty to advise that there was no legal claim. It occurred to me that the case was not one in which there was property damage within the meaning of the Act, and I had to advise the department that I did not think they could entertain the ciaim. Then the matter came up by way of petition of right. The reverend gentleman applied for a petition of right to have his position settled by judgment of the court. I immediately acquiesced in that and a petition of right was granted. The judgment of the Exchequer Court was in his favour. The judge of the Exchequer Court held that the man's property had been injuriously affected and its value decreased and that as a result the government should pay for the damage. He fixed the amount at $1,200. I remained still of the opinion-being perhaps obdurate in this matter-that the judgment of the Exchequer Court was wrong and I advised an appeal to the Supreme Court. When the case came before the Supreme Court they concurred in my view, namely, that while the right of access had been interfered with, the man's property had not been injuriously affected so as to give him a claim for damages. I have no recollection of having seen any recommendation in the judgment that we should pay the costs of the appeal to the Supreme Court. If my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) is satisfied from his own personal knowledge that this recommendation is contained in the judgment I shall have it looked up and certainly such a recommendation as that should receive and would receive the sympathetic consideration of the government. If they recommend that in this case the suppliant should have his costs paid, I do not think the government would hesitate a moment to adopt such a suggestion. My hon. friend says that, the Supreme Court having decided that this gentleman is not entitled to consideration, in the way of remuneration for the damage he has suffered, that we should appeal that question to the Privy Council. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that we cannot take the appeal.
He will take it if you pay the costs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If he takes the appeal we will give him every possible facility. He cannot appeal except on application for leave. If he applies for leave I shall agree that leave be granted, but when he comes and asks us that we should assume the burden of taking an appeal and as-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
sume all the costs the question arises what principle we are to lay down. The hon. gentleman says that he will not consider it a precedent but while he does not and will not, other gentlemen in the same position may do so, and may come to us and say : Treat us in the same way ; appeal to the Privy Council at your expense and for our benefit. I do not see what answer we could make in such a case, nor do I see how the government could justify any suggestion to take the case to the Privy Council by way of paying the costs. There is no principle at stake ; it is one of those cases that come before the court every day, a question of whether the damage to a man's property is such as would entitle him to recover damages. I do not see why we should distinguish between this minister's case and other cases. I can understand my hon. friend's sympathy for his constituent, [DOT] and I quite appreciate his desire to secure relief for him. He says that this case is one of hardship. I admit that it is a hard case but so far as I am concerned I can only apply the law. I could not pay damages in such a case nor could I advise the government to do so. My hon. friend says that there is a recommendation in the judgment as to costs. I repeat that if there is such a recommendation as to costs I shall consider it and have it complied with. Of course I have not looked at the judgment recently.

At the time the judgment was given I just noticed a paragraph that appeared in the newspaper, probably three or four lines, in the way they generally report these cases, and I should judge from the wording of that paragraph that the judgment contained some recommendation that the government should pay the costs. I am only speaking of what I saw in the newspaper.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course I am now speaking only from -my impression. It is some weeks since I read the judgment. My impression was that the court held that the suppliant would not be obliged to pay the costs of the Crown on the appeal, that each party would have to pay his own costs.

I am not sure, but, on rendering it, I came to the conclusion that the court suggested that the government should pay the costs. The minister has just stated that on this case several others depended, and that others were pushing this case through. I may say to the minister that there was no one connected with this gentleman at all ; he has paid his own costs and I do not think there is a single solitary person who has put up one dollar for him. He has had to pay all his costs in connection with the case so far, but is unable to proceed as he has not the means to do so, and therefore he has to suffer this hardship. I venture to say that I can

.say for the whole village-and at all events I would do so before I would ask the government to allow the ease to go to appeal- that they would pledge themselves that they would not regard this as a precedent. But of course if judgment were given in favour of the reverend gentleman, then they could have their own cases tried and if necessary could take them to the Privy Council. Of course there is no question that there are quite a few others who would be in a similar position, and there is no doubt that there would be others who would have to be paid if the government settled this one claim. This gentleman, in the eyes of the public in the locality, is entitled to damages, and in view of the fact that he got judgment from the court that is supposed to settle these cases and that it was only on a technical point that the Supreme Court decided against him, I feel now that the least the government could do would be to make a grant of a few hundred dollars in order that justice might be done this gentleman and others. There is no question about it in my own opinion- and I believe in the opinion of the public in that locality,-that this gentleman has been most unfairly dealt with in so far as his property is concerned. That is the reason that I make this appeal, which I suppose is the last appeal X can make. I have appealed to the Minister of Railways, and the Minister of Justice. I appeal to the Prime Minister, and I am very sorry they cannot grant that request and allow this reverend gentleman to get the amount to which he is entitled. I believe the least they could do would be to pay him the $1,200 to which he is entitled, without making it a precedent. The government could buy his property for a few hundred dollars more than the damages, and could use it for some of the lockmen or for some other purpose. There is a way of getting over it I am sure. It would be as easy to get over that as to get over the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill. I think it would not be much trouble and I am now making this last appeal to the Prime Minister, to the Minister of Justice and to the Minister of Railways to see if they cannot find some means of doing something by which he will get the justice to which I believe he is entitled.

I suggest that they take for this purpose a portion of the money they are paying out for trimmings, that do not require to be done. I would ask the minister if he can tell us how much of this money which we are voting is to be used for paying what is already earned, by work having been done and how much is yet to be earned and the kind of work that is to be done to earn it.
It is practically all earned.
If that be so then the work must be completed.
I have explained to my hon. friend that we are just doing the finishing up work. When I say it is practically all earned I do not mean to say that every dollar is earned.
I understand that it will take about $15,000 more to complete this ?

About $30,000, according to the last report we have from the engineer, who 'has died since. That was made out about three weeks ago.
1 Mr. SPROiJLE. Then I suppose the whole staff of engineers will be kept on until that is spent.
As soon as the work is through, the staff will be reduced.
I would suggest that as soon as the elections come on this man should put in his claim, provided the others do the same.
Does the hon. Minister of Justice remember if t'he Supreme Court were unanimous in that case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not remember. I will look into the case, because it is important to know whether there was such a recommendation as has been suggested by my hon. friend.
North channel-forming channel and dam, $150,000.

This amount is to continue and complete the forming of a channel above the Galops canal. This channel is 2* miles long, 300 feet wide and 10 feet deep. It is also for the building of a dam between Galops and Adams Islands. By building this dam a dangerous bar is removed, making the navigation more safe. To complete the work under contract, including the dam, requires $150,000. The total amount expended on t'he work to the 1st of May, 1904, is $1,314,000.42.
What was the estimated cost of it, and what will be the total amount expended when it is completed ?
The total cost will be $1,464,000.
What was the estimated cost of the channel and the dam separately by the department when the first vote was taken ?

The original estimate of making a 2o0 foot channel was three quarters of a million dollars. The estimated cost of the dam was in the vicinity of $60,000. But the channel was increased to 300 feet in width, and therefore the cost has been very largely increased.
Was that after the contract was let ?
Yes, but the work was at schedule prices.
Who had the contract ?
Cleveland.

You spent last year $85,-
000.
It was paid to the contractors on account of the contract.
If the dam is now completed, what has it cost ?
It is not finally completed.
How much has been spent on the dam ?
I have not the information as to the dam separately. The deputy thinks the estimate has been exceeded.
And yet the work is not finished. I think this item should not pass until we get that information. I am not objecting to the building of this dam. It was built last year.
There are 300 feet of it in whic*h the cribs have not yet been sunk. The progress estimates as they are received are in one amount for both the channel and the dam.
You do not separate the estimates between the channel and the dam'.
No, because it is all one contract.
They are a mile apart.
They might be two miles apart. They are all one contract a! schedule prices, and the progress estimates are sent in on the work without regard to whether it is the dam or the channel.
If it is on progress estimates and the minister took an amouni last year to complete the whole, why is he coming now and asking for $150,000 ?
This is to complete the work under the contract.
Does the hon. minister tell us that this dam is part of the original contract ?
Yes.
Surely not. It was not contemplated then.
I am bound by the information which I get from my officials.
This contract was lei some seven or eight years ago. Are we to understand that at that time this dam was contemplated and made part of this contract ?
Yes; there has been no other contract.
This is done on American soil. Have you got the consent of the Americans to the building of it ?
Yes.
I may say to the hon. minister that so far as this dam is concerned, I never heard of it and it was not talked of nor contemplated when this contract was let.
It might have been contemplated without the hon. gentleman hearing of it.

In the contract there is nothing specified aboult bulilding a dam.
If there was to be a dam, would it not be specified in the contract? The contract is very plain, and it only provides for dredging and some piering at the west end of the channel. I know the contractor well, and you could not get a better one. I am not finding fault with this contractor or his work. The only question I have asked is how much has been spent on this dam. The minister tells us that the prices allowed the contractor are just the same as on the other dredging work. I suppose that means tne cribwork is so much per foot and the dredging or filling in so much per yard, the same as tlie original contract.
Yes, under the original contract.
I mean that for the work done at the head of the channel, the same prices are paid as across this dam ?
That is what my deputy tells me.
And the two are not kept separate ?
No ; the vote is asked for the channel and the dam. It was that way last year.

This was all done last fall. The Auditor General's Report could not show whether they were separate or not. because all this work has been done since July 1st of last year as far as this dam is concerned. That is why we are entitled to some information now.
My deputy tells me that he could get the information by figuring it out.

When we are on the supplementaries, will the minister be in a [DOT] position to state how much has been paid on the dam so far and. how much he expects it will cost to complete ? I may say that I believe this dam across the island has had the effect of turning the water back and throwing it around the head of the island, by which I believe it will do some good in so far as the entrance into the head of the canal is concerned. It has increased the water so that boats can enter the head of

the canal more easily. X know it was a difficult work, and the contractor has done it well. Still I think we are entitled to know exactly what it cost.
Have there been any complaints from overflow from this dam ?
None.
The hon. minister did not answer my question. Last year there was a vote of $60,000. He says that the dam and the north channel were both included in the contract. $60,000 was voted last year.
Any way, it was to finish the work. How is it that $100,000 more is asked this year ?
Nearly $150,000 more. There must be some mistake if such a statement was made.

Here it is in ' Hansard ' :
To complete the north channel (revote), $20,000.
You say that thjit was part and parcel of the whole contract, that the dam was made a portion of it. Then the discussion went on :
Does that complete the work ?
Yes. I wish to amend that item by adding the words ' and dam between Galops and Adam's island.'
Will this complete the Cleveland work on the north channel ?
Yes, that is the report of the engineers.
And the dam, too ?
Yes, we are so advised.
That is pretty explicit.
What has the department to say ?

I will have to take
back what was said last year.
Does the hon. minister not see that if we cannot secure exact information about these things it is a perfect farce our asking for information ?

The Finance Minister was acting Minister of Railways last year. Let me read again the question asked him :
To complete north channel (revote),
Does that complete the work ?
Yes. I wish to amend that item by adding the words 1 and dam between Galops and Adam's island.'
Will this complete the Cleveland work on the north channel ?
Yes, that is the report of the engineers.
And the dam, too T

Yes, we are so advised.
Yet now we are asked to vote another $150,000, and the Minister of Railways says that the work on the dam is not half through, and that the work on the channel is likely to continue for some time yet. What has the Minister of Finance to say regarding that statement which he made last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only say that at that time, as the information the hon. gentleman has read shows, I stated that we were so advised by the engineer, and I am quite sure that I had the engineer's opinion to that effect or I would not have made the statement. I am told by the Minister of Railways that Mr. Rubidge did make such a recommendation at that time.
He's dead.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, we cannot extend the lives even of worthy men for ever. 1 take it for granted that the minister to-day is asking for this sum on the report of the engineer.	-
Will the hon. minister bring down that report ?
I will.
Only $20,000 was asked a year ago to complete this work, and now $150,000 is asked to complete it. Perhaps we could get an estimate of what it will really take to complete the work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is a growing time.
Has the minister had a special engineer's report on this work-any engineer other than one in his own department?
No, it was under the control of Mr. Rubidge, who was the superintending engineer-
That is no answer to give to the committee. The department is answerable for the expenditure so long as they retain the parties on whose advice they act.

Certainly-no one man denies that. But I was asked whether any special engineer was asked to make a report on the matter, and I am endeavouring to enlighten my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) on that particular point. I was endeavouring to say that there was no special engineer, that the only engineer who made a report was Mr. Rubidge, the chief superintending engineer.

I would draw the hon. minister's attention to this statement at page 4034 of ' Hansard ' of 1902. This was in the discussion on the item ' North channel, forming dam $56,250. ' My hon. friend from

Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) made the statement that this was useless expenditure.
So it is-altogether.
And my hon. friend the former Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Haggart) repeats that statement.
I understand my hon. friend from Grenville 'to have changed his opinion with respect to it and to say now that it is a work of value.

I have not changed my mind on anything. I am under the impression that my hon friend (Mr. Blain) is refer-ii'ing to a matter that comes up on the next item relating to Galops Rapids. So far as this channel is concerned. I believe it is absolutely necessary and that it is a good work. Mr. M. A. Cleveland, who has been working on it, I believe is a first-class contractor and .has done his work well. I do not believe there is a better contractor on the canal than Mr. Cleveland. But I recall the fact that, last year, when the question was asked if the $20,000 then voted would finish up the work, we were told that it would, let. this year the minister comes down'and asks for $150,000, and this we are asked to vote without any explanation whatever, except a statement by the Minister of Railways and Canals which virtually means that there will be more money required. That is the position we are in to-day. The minuter cannot tell us whether this ends the contract, or whetuer the work will finish this year, next year or five years hence. Personally, I feel that we have not received the information that would justify even a lot of school boys in approving this expenditure. much less the House of Commons of Canada which has the interest of the whole people in its charge.

My hon. friend (Mr. ,T. D. Reid) says that this is an excellent work and that the contractor has done good work. My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) says that the expenditure upon it is a waste of money.
He is referring to the Galops Rapids.
No, I am referring to the north channel. I stated it before in the House, and I feel justified in repeating it, for the work came under my observation.
Well, which is right- my hon. friend from South Lanark or my hon. friend from Grenville ? How can 1 tell ?

I may say that the hon. member for South Lanark will explain that. From the head of the canal at Cardinal to Prescott, according to the old channel where the boats have run for the last thirty or forty years there were spots in it where there was only eight or nine feet of water, and

the question was whether it was better to make a new channel where it is now or dredge the old channel to the necessary depth. My opinion of the matter as expressed, was that the work as now done when completed was a work of actual necessity, or else the old channel had to be dredged. There may be difference of opinion as to which was the best route to take. I am not discussing that point and I do not know whether I could form an opinion upon it. But deeper water was necessary in order to accommodate the boats drawing 16 or 17 feet of water coming from Montreal. And, [that depth having been secured I say the work is a good work so far as the interest of navigation is concerned.

I suppose I too must keep myself right in this matter. I made the statement a moment ago that my hon. friend from Grenville condemned the expenditure, and I suppose I must give the evidence. At page 4034 of 'Hansard' of 1902. in the course of the discussion on the item ' North Channel, forming dank $56,250 ; the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Reid) said : '
It is simply throwing til is away. Better throw the money into the canal than throw a dam across there.
I understand the hon. gentleman now to say that he was directing attention to another matter, and so I will not debate that.
Mr. EMMERSoN. It is a difference between the hon. gentlemen themselves and I am quite willing to let them settle it.

My hon. friend "(Mr. J. D. Reid) has explained that Ms remarks referred to something else, and of course, I accept bis statement, as the minister is bound also to do. A little while ago I asked if any engineer outside of the department had made a report on this work and his answer was in the negative. I wish to draw his attention to what his predecessor, Hon. Mr. Blair says. Speaking in answer to a question as to the expenditure, he said :
I will tell the hon. gentleman what I will do. I will undertake that the money will not be expended until I have the subject thoroughly investigated, and until 'I have had the opinion ot other engineers. Not being an engineer myself, I cannot form a judgment upon a question of this kind. I can, however, probably decide not to spend, and I will not do so until I ascertain from independent engineers that it would be a proper expenditure to make.
There is a clear and distinct statement by Mr. Blair when he was asking for this vote of $56,250. It was questioned by this side of the House, and the minister pledged his word to the committee that not one cent of increased expenditure would be made until he had consulted another and outside independent engineer. The committee accepted his word and let the item go through. The

money was expended, and now my hon. friend comes forward and asks us for $150,000. He also makes the further statement that that sum will not complete the work.
No, I stated that I -was advised that this $150,000 will complete the work.
The dam as well as the channel V
Both.
The minister stated that a short while ago.
I said that it would take $30,000 to complete the previous work.

Upon that statement in 1902 by the minister who had charge of the department, the money was voted and expended. Now coming to last year, in addition to what the member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) has read, on the same item ' North channel-forming channel and dam,' the Minister of Finance said that the total cost of that work when completed would be $1,354,410 including the dam. Now we have already expended $110,000 more than that. Then the Minister of Finance went on to say that there was a further appropriation of $18,000, and that these two items would complete the work. These are the promises that we get. This thing is of a daily and hourly occurrence in this House. The government come forward with an estimate, the minister stands behind the engineer and pledges his word that the sum asked for will complete the work. I do not think any member on this side of the House would expect that an engineer could make an exact estimate of what a work of that kind would cost, I do not think that is possible. But [DOT]when the government come forward and state that an estimate is based upon an engineer's opinion, one whose duty it is to make a report upon that work, and then, year after year, they come before this committee and ask for increased amounts with the statement that the sum previously voted will not complete the work, then 1 say that the committee have a right to complain of the government. The difficulty rests somewhere with the government. On this side of the House we have nothing to do with the officers of the government ; the people and the opposition have no one to hold responsible except the ministers. It is time the ministers became more careful in the statements they make. It is the wish of the opposition to deal fairly with the government. I must say that we expect the Minister of the Department of Railways, who is new in his department, to do better than his predecessor. I am sorry to see, however, that he is not starting in very well. I would ask him to be more careful in the statements and promises he makes to the committee.

In addition to what the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has read from the statements of the minister in 1902,
I will read what I said in 1903 :
Before the committee rises, I wish to say that I shall have some remarks to make on items No. 91 and No. 92, referring to the forming of a dam in the north channel on the Galops rapids. The minister is aware that I took exception to the building of the dam, because it was part and parcel of that new channel. In discussing the matter with the marine men since, they state that they believe that the building of -that dam will overcome the great damage that has been done to the water-way by the deepening of that channel, thus causing the lowering of the water above the island. They think that this wrong which I claim has been done for a great many years, would be really overcome by the building of this dam. I do not intend now to object to the building of that dam. I believe it will probably raise the water again to its normal level as it was previous to this work being done.
That shows that I did make these remarks in 1902. and in 1903 I corrected them. So there is no dispute.

['Before the committee rises I would ask the minister if he would kindly leave one item on the Trent Valley canal for discussion until Wednesday. I am obliged to be absent on Monday and Tuesday.\nSome resolutions reported.']

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At six o'clock we were discussing item 95, $150,000 for the north channel.

As was stated in the House when this item was under discussion there was an item of $20,000 in the supple-mentaries last year in addition to $80,000 in the main estimates, making $100,000 in all. The Minister of Finance stated that this $20,000 would complete the whole work on that north channel. He justified himself by having an estimate from the chief engineer on that particular work. This chief engineer subsequently sent a report to the department in which he stated that it would require $150,000 additional. As I understand from the minister now this $150,000 is intended to complete the whole of that north channel and that dam, and the report of the department is to that effect. The department obtained a certificate from the chief engineer or the engineer who was directly in charge of that work-and this was communicated to this House by the minister in charge of the estimates-that this would complete the work ; the engineer subsequently gave a certificate that it would require $150,000 more. The minister made some criticism of my statement that the north channel was an entirely useless one and compared it with the statement of the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid). When that item was first brought up it was brought before me as Minister of Railways and I refused absolutely to support the contention of the engineer as to the necessity of that work. I say that it is an absolutely useless expenditure of money. My contention at the time was that by deepening what is called Pier Island shoal you could have got a proper entrance into the Galops canal, for one half of the amount that is being expended now for an entrance. The objection taken by the minister at that time was that we would have to use the American channel. The American channel from the Pier Island shoal up to Prescott has a depth of thirty feet. Past Pier Island shoal, there was no necessity of deepening the river at all. He said you would be getting into American waters. My answer Mr. HYMAN.
was that under the Treaty of Washington, we have as much right to utilize and navigate the American portion of the St. Lawrence as the Americans have themselves, and they have an equal right to utilize and navigate our portion. My contention was that there was no need at all of the expenditure, [DOT] which is in the neighbourhood of $1,400,000 ; and now it is proposed to expend $150,000 more, a total expenditure of about $1,600,000 to do what I contend could have been accomplished by an expenditure at the utmost of $100,000. From that time to the present I have never changed my opinion that this expenditure for the purpose of building the north channel is entirely useless. It was contended that perhaps the water passing over the Galops rapids would prevent barges or ships coming down from making the entrance to the Galops canals. But you must remember that you have erected a dam between two islands, where I suggested that the shoal should be deepened, and the canal, which did away altogether with that danger. But what I want to draw the minister's particular attention to is the former part of my statement. After having a certificate from the engineer in charge of the work that $20,000 would complete it, he receives a subsequent one that it will require $150,000 more. Have the officers of the department communicated with the engineer in charge of the work and got from him a reason for his change of opinion ?

The late engineer, Mr. Rubidge, in his lifetime was asked that question by the department. His explanation was not in writing, and my attention was not called to it. I cannot give any personal explanation ; but I will take the earliest opportunity to examine the situation and learn exactly where the difliculty lies and where the fault is if there has been fault. That is the only thing that I can do at this time, and I shall endeavour to get that information from sources that will not be considered as in any way prejudiced.

I do not say the minister ought to have done it, but the department ought to have done it. The department had a report from Mr. Rubidge that $20,000 would finish the work and it put that statement in the mouth of the minister in charge of the department at that time. Then a subsequent report came in that $150,000 more would be required. The minister's attention ought to have been called to that. The department ought to have got the information without the minister inquiring into the matter at all.

When the hon. member for South Lanark was Minister of Railways and Canals, if my memory serves me rightly, the government of that day were asking for tenders for enlarging the Cardinal canal and also for a channel from the head of the

canal to Prescott. The intention of the minister was to have the rock excavated at Pier Island shoal and at the same time to run the canal through the village of Cardinal much further south than where it is and where it would not have injured the village and would have been a straight canal. The intention was to run the canal straight from what is known as the upper lock almost to Iroquois. If that had been done, the canal would have been straight, and it would have cost only about one-half of what it has cost as located. But just at that time the government changed, and the Hon. Mr. Blair became Minister of Railways and Canals. Without ever appearing on the scene he changed the route of the canal and located it where it now is. I was informed at the time that the late Mr. Rubidge strongly urged the southern route. If the minister asks the deputy minister, I believe he will agree with me that the canal where it passes through the village of Cardinal, and where it was intended to be made straight, is about as crooked as the old original canal. If the minister visits it he will see that the canal there has a large curve ; but it has been made much wider and deeper, so that boats can navigate it more easily than they could the old canal. But, as the hon. member for South Lanark states, west of the canal there was only a small shoal to be removed to make a channel twenty or thirty feet in depth from the head of the canal to Prescott, and the work could have been done for perhaps $100,000 or $150,000.
But, of course, in doing this the vessel would have had to go some 500 or 600 feet in American waters. None of the excavating work, however, would have had to be done in American waters. That canal had been used for forty years, and a vessel could have entered it easily, because it could have got around this island half a mile above the entrance and have plenty of opportunity to go into the canal. But for the same reason, this route was changed and was made to cur. right through the island. They had to remove half the island. The water was only five or six feet deep in most of the channel, and as this, channel had to be dredged, there is no question but that it could not be done without an enormous expenditure, as has been proved by the expenditure from that time to this. Of course, either one route or the other had to be made. The government were compelled to either remove the shoal near the island or do what they have done now. What has been done makes a splendid channel, but in doing this the govern ment have squandered at least a million dollars, which it would not have been necessary to spend had they gone through the old channel and allowed the vessels to navigate its waters as they had been doing for so many years. Therefore, the ex-Minister of Railways is perfectly right in what he says regarding this expenditure. Another matter I wish to mention is this. These canals are
now completed. At any rate, they are all in working order. Take the Cardinal canal. In that there is one lock less, and as it is just new and complete, it should be operated for much less than during the Conservative regime or up to the time the present government took power in 1896. Well, what do we find ? I find that previous to the year 1896 it cost to manage those canals as follows:	Take the Williamsburg canal,
it cost for the permanent staff, $9,567.09 ; and for the actual repairs to keep it in working order, $7,123.97. That included Farran's Point, Morrisburg and Cardinal canals. In 1903. although the canals were new, just handed over by the contractor and in splendid working order, and when it might be supposed that they could not require repairs to anything like the amount they did in 1896, I find that the expenditure of the staff increased from $9,567 in 1895 to $15,246.91. And for the repairs to those canals it cost $7,123.97 to keep them in repair in 1895, and in 1903 it cost $20,092.79. From the first day the Liberals came into office the expenditure on those canals has increased, so that there is not one year which does not show an increase over the previous year. Take the Cornwall -canal, in 1896 it "cost $15,114.56 for what is known as the staff, but last year it cost $70,129.29, or an increase from $15,000 per annum to $70,000. Of course, in that latter amount is included lighting, $48,000, which I am not going to discuss now, because that will come up on a special item later, but in the year 1895 that was also included in the $15,400. Compare that with last year, and you will find that, leaving the lighting out of last year's expenditure, the cost of operating the canal was $22,129.29, as compared with $15,400 in 1895, and that latter amount included the lighting. The repairs on these new canals cost $19,235 last year, while in 1895 they only cost $13,053.53. Then take the Lnchine canal, which, in 1895, was an old canal. In that year the staff cost $56,185.44, whereas in 1903 it cost $69,534.56. And for the repairs on this old canal, in 1895 it cost $24,924 89, whereas in 1903, on the new canal, the repairs cost $53,054.20, or more #ian double. Take the Sault Ste. Marie canal. In 1895 that canal cost $3,432.03 for staff. Tt is only a short canal with one lock, yet in 1903 it cost for the staff to manage that lock $16,017.22. And for the repairs on that little piece of canal it cost in 1903 $10,855.70, so that in 1903 it took $27,000 to run one lock on the Sault canal, while in 1895 the extravagant Conservative government managed to run it for $3,432. Take the Welland canal. In 1895 the staff of that canal cost $89,065.27, while in 1903 it cost $90,290.65. And the repairs on the whole length of the Welland canal in 1895 cost $40,270.94, as compared with $72,004.59 in 1903. You can take every canal throughout this Dominion and you will find that the cost of management and repairs has increased almost two-

fold under the present government. Take the canal that I know well, the one in my own county ; X cannot see any necessity for employing more men to keep it in repair at present than under the late government.
