Why, on the contrary, there should be only one-half of the repairs required to-day, and yet the minister, if he will take up his paylist, will find that he has three times as many employees looking after the repairs, and if the Auditor General's Report were ready we would find that there are men employed on that canal the whole year who, I believe, did not work one day.
And I see item after item charged to these canals representing expenditure for which I can see no justification whatever. Take this Cardinal canal from Iroquois to the head of the rapids, it had only been 'handed over by the contractor and not a dollar (had to be spent, so far as X can see for repairs. There should have been no charge for repairs for three years, because the contractors had full charge of the banks and were emptying upon them the material that they excavated. I cannot see why there should be such a great expense in managing this canal as in former years. If you go over the expenditure on these canals for thirty years, whether the Liberals were in power or whether the Conservatives were in power, you will find that it remained about the same year after year-only a few hundred dollars difference either way. But on this canal it is increasing year by year the same on the Weland canal, the same on the Lachine canal, the same on the Cornwall canal and the Soulanges and Beauharnois canals as well. Is this increase to go on every year ? Every time the Liberal committee meets in Iroquois or Cardinal and sends a recommendation for two more men or four more men to be put on the canal, or for certain supplies to be bought from certain men, must the minister load this expenditure upon the country regardless of the public interest ? These men are put there and they cannot be dismissed, and the government will take no action in the matter. We had an example this afternoon when the minister admitted to me that he had men employed on the engineering staff that, to my knowledge, tiave had nothing to do but draw their salaries. Then there is the coj-lector of canal tolls at Cardinal. Not a dollar of canal tolls was collected last year, yet the collector was paid for a full twelve months $1,000. Not only that, but he was paid $1 per day for driving from the village up to the locks to his office, where he had not anything to do. And in addition to that, he was paid office rent down at .his own house. In addition to that, he was paid for fuel. And, in addition to all. he was paid 20 cents an hour for extra work on Sundays, though the canal was closed from twelve o'clock on Saturday night to twelve o'clock Mr. J D. REID.
on Sunday night. The Auditor General's Report shows this, and it seems all the more noteworthy because the collectors on the other canals have not received anything for extra work. Will the minister explain why this extravagance exists, why these officials are kept, why horse-hire is paid, and rent and fuel and all these other things? And, so far as this collector of whom I have spoken is concerned, he has just one thing to do in connection with his position and that is to go to the post office at tfhe end of the month and get his cheque.

I have heard my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) deliver this speech more than once. It seems to grow in intensity as the figures increase year by year. I fancy that after a while, he will begin to think there really is something in it. He forgets, of course, that, in the days of progress in Canada, when trade is, figuratively speaking, doubling year by year, necessarily the canals get a share of the increased traffic, and this, of course, involves additional expense in operation. These canals have been enlarged. He refers to a section of the Cornwall canal and says that the expense is nearly double what it was. I am informed that, in the meantime the number of locks has been doubled, and, of course, that involves greater expense.
i Mr. J. D. REID. I would like to know who gave that information to the hon. minister. I do not think any officer of the department will say that the number of locks Isas been increased.
I am informed by the deputy minister that the number has been doubled.
On what canal ?

On the Cornwall canal, the one to which my hon. friend refers, Turning to the records, I find that, at page 12 of the report of the Department of Railways and Canals of last year, that the cost of staff on the Cornwall canal for 1895, was $15,414.56, and for repairs, $13,000 odd, while, for 1902-that is previous to the lighting, which is another question-the cost for staff was only $17,896.58, a very small increase over 1895, while for repairs only $15,000, again a very small increase, especially when you take into consideration the enlargement of the canal.
Compare the Williamsburg canal. The Cornwall canal happens to be one of the smallest increased.
I am taking one that the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Reid) started with.
No. I started with the Williamsburg.
But the hon. gentleman made reference to the Cornwall canal.
The hon. minister states that there are more locks on the Cornwall .canal with the new canal than with the old canal in 1896. I challenge that statement.	[DOT]

The statement I made was that there were a great many more now than before the enlargement was made. The enlargement was only completed two or three years ago. My hon. friend has called attention to the Williamsburg canal and has shown that there is an increase. But taking into consideration the large increase of business, the enlargement of the canal and the increased cost of management, also taking into consideration that the present government pay living wages, whereas under the former regime people received starvation wages-I say that taking all these things into consideration, the additional work that is being done, the increased traffic that is attended to, we must expect an increase in the cost of operation. My hon. friend went on to speak about the locks in the canal. I was a little shocked at his contending that it would be in the interest of Canada to have a canal in American territory. If that proposition were to come from this side of the House it would be denounced as traitorous, as disloyal, and I am a little surprised at my hon. friend even making that suggestion. If it came from any other quarter he would be horrified, but in order to make a point against the government he now advocates that we should have a portion of this canal in American territory instead of having it all upon Canadian soil. Personally I know nothing of the locality, and am not in a position to form a judgment upon it, except from the facts recited by my hon. friend. From what I can gather from the member for South Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) the differences between the hon. gentlemen have been adjusted.
Did I state that a part of it was on American soil 1
Some of the boats going through there would have to go through American territory as I understand it. But I did not charge the hon. member for South Lanark with saying that.

I said a boat coming from the head of the canal would have to go through American waters. If the minister is so loyal, how is it that a vessel cannot go between Prescott and Kingston without going through American waters 1

My hon. friend should not be so impetuous. I am pointing out that evidently since recess the little differences that existed between my hon. friends have been amicably adjusted, and they seem to harmonize once more regarding the Cornwall canal.
Remember Shakespeare's motto about brevity. For goodness' sake, be short.
I am perhaps imitating my hon. friends.
A good dinner is supposed to lubricate business.
I should take occasion to inquire into the figures presented by my hon. friend and may have occasion to refer to them.

The minister says that he would be accused of disloyalty if he advocated the proposition of the ex-Minister of Railways. I drew the attention of this government year after year to the fact that if they went on with the work at the Galops Rapids, it would have to be all done in American territory. Notwithstanding that fact, they are now paying money for dredging that is all done in American territory. The next item that follows this asks for money to be spent in dredging a channel through American territory. Any boat that ever entered that channel must necessarily go through American territory, either going down or coming up the river. In this case his loyalty is not so great as it is in the other, where the expenditure has already been made. Now the minister says that the increased cost of operation is owing to the increase of business and the employment of a larger staff. I make this statement, that there are no more locks on the Cardinal canal or on the Williamsburg canal than there were in 1895. On the Farran's Point canal there was one lock in 1896, and there is only one to-day, the only difference is" that it has been enlarged.
There are two locks on the Farran's Point canal, the old one and the new one.
The old one was taken away, no boat goes through that.
Then it is a question of veracity between my hon. friend and (lie superintendent of the canal and the deputy minister. I assume that my hon. friend is labouring under softie misapprehension.
That is news to me. I have gone up and down the canal very often. Then there were two locks on the Williamsburg canal in 1896 and there are two locks to-day. Is that right ?
That is right. You have struck it for once.
On the Cardinal canal there were three locks in 1896, and there are two now. Am I right in that ?
Three on the Galops.

When the Cardinal canal was built there was only one lock at Iroquois, one at Cardinal and one at the head of the



canal. The new lock at Iroquois was built much higher so that they could do away with the lock at Cardinal and there was this new lock built at the head of the canal. The level between Iroquois and the head of the canal is now the same and there Is one lock less. The old lock around by the other way has been abandoned, there is no reason why an official of any kind should be employed on that lock, so that when the hon. minister speaks of that as one lock, he refers to a lock at Which there is not one dollar expended and at which there is not an official. I would like to know where the other lock is on the Iroquois canal if there are three.

In the chief engineer's report the mileage of the Galops canal Is given as 71 miles and the number of locks as three. That does not include this old lock to which my hon. friend refers. There is one at Iroquois, the large lock which is mentioned, and at the head, or the entrance, there are two locks.
It El It. There are two locks together but the same crew manage them.
That makes three locks.
Well, there are two together.
It is not a question as to the number of men. I was speaking as to the number of locks.
That is another lock on the outside. I did not get that far.
You were right before but you seem to have missed that one.

I said there were two locks at the head of the canal going west. There are only two there, one less than there was before. Then, there is another lock going down on the outside of the river. That makes three.
Then there is the old lock.
In the first place it is necessary to continue the collectors at these points in order that a record may be kept.
Of what ?

The making of the canals free to the people for a period of years is an experiment so that it may be tested. In the meantime it is necessary to have a record and these men are employed. They have to give their time in the same way even though the government do not collect tolls. I think an answer to all that has been said by my hon. friend can be found in the report of the Department of Railways and Canals for 1903, part II, page 25. The hon. gentleman refers to the Sault Ste. Marie canal. I find that in 1895 there was a payment of $3,432.73 for staff. The canal had only been opened for a month or so during the year so that that is not for a year's operation. In 1896 it cost $10,074.70 for staff. In 1903 at the same place it cost $16,077.22 for staff. There is an increase of $2.30.

You have struck it right this time.
JUiLY 8, 1904
X strike It right every time when it comes to figures.
No, you do not.

My hon. friend knows that under the system in vogue along the canals the operators get an increased wage over that paid by the former government and they also get a free house or house rental allowed. These increased wages must necessarily be taken into consideration.
Did they not get house rent before ?
I am informed not.
They always got a government house on the other canals free before.
Only a very few.
On the Williamsburg canal they always have had government houses free of rent.

I am informed that some of them received that, but that it was not general. Since this government came into power it has been made general, and therefore the cost to the country has increased. The cost of material for repairs has been increased. Wherever lumber has to be used the expense is much greater. Generally labour for repairs is much more expensive now than it was, so that there is very little in what my hon. friend has said.

I know for a fact that prior to 1896 every lockmaster and lock labourer on the Williamsburg canal either had a free house or was allowed, I think, ?50 per annum to pay for a rented house. That was the case all along the Williamsburg canal.
I said there were some instances, but that that system did not prevail on the canals generally. My hon. friend was making a charge as to the increased expense all along the canal system.
I would like the minister to make his statement definite, in order that I may make inquiries so that we can discuss it next session.
I shall have a complete list prepared.

The hon. gentleman has stated that there has been an increased traffic on these canals. Would he give us a statement of the number of vessels that passed through during the season of navigation of 1903 and the season of 1896 ?

I was rather assuming that the traffic would be greater in these years than before. I do not think that that argument is very material when I come to reflect on it, because the men have to be there, night and day* whether one vessel or twenty pass through the canal during the 202
twenty-four hours. It may be that while the number of boats has not increased, owing to the fact that larger boats are used, a great deal more freight is carried through the canals, as one boat now will carry as much as half a dozen would in years gone by. The canals have been deepened in many instances, and therefore can accommodate a larger class of boats ; but, after all, so far as the staff is concerned, the number of boats is not material.
I would like the minister to bring down with the other statement a list showing the number of boats passing through the canals in 1896 and 1903.
I will get one for all of the seasons ; it would be an interesting record.
I understand that the government have arranged to open and close the gates on the Cornwall canal by electricity.

They propose to.
Mr. ,1. D. REID. Are they doing it now ? Yet the staff has been increased ; there are more men on the locks than in 1896, when they had to open the gates by hand power.

I do not think that is the case, but I will get the statistics for my own satisfaction. I think they are taking into consideration the question of the advisability of reducing the number of hands in view of the use of electrical power.

In 1896 on the Cornwall canal they had a lockmaster and four men on account of boats running both ways up and down. Now they have the electrical power, and, as I understand, one man is supposed to manage the whole affair, because there is nothing to do, and yet there are more men on each lock than there were in 1S96 when the men had to open the locks with a windlass. I understand that the number of employees has been increased.
I shall obtain that information.

It is apparent that the government have increased the cost of opening and shutting the gates in the Cornwall canal very materially since 1896. I would ask the minister when the supplementaries come up for discussion to bring down these statements for which we have asked, so that we can go into this matter again.
Galops rapids-to complete channel, $40,000.

This is a revote of $40,000, the unexpended portion of $75,000 which was appropriated last year. This is to complete the formation of the channel in the Galops rapids. A large amount of drilling and blasting has been done, but the material has not been excavated. The work is being done by the Gilbert Company. The channel is 3,000 feet long, 200 feet wide and



17 feet deep. The amount expended up to ttie 1st of May, 1904, was, $878,441.35. The estimated cost of completing the channel, including this $40,000, is $75,000, that is, assuming that an estimate made in February last that $35,000 of the $75,000 would be expended before the 30th of June, 1904, turns out to have been correct.

I have been in this House now some thirteen years, and each and every year the minister gets up and makes the same statement, that it will take some $40,000 or $50,000 to complete this channel, and that it will be completed within the next year, wrhen the fact is that this ijs just being carried on in the interest of the contractors. Does the minister know when this work was started ? It was started by the Mackenzie government in 1878, to make a new channel to allow large vessels to go through, and it is not ready yet. If we are to wait until these contractors will have it ready, the minister can make up his mind to wait-for another quarter of a century.
Mr. EMMERiaON. Was the contract entered into in 1878 1

I think that was the year in which it was started, and they have been working at it ever since with the exception of two or three years. I would like to ask the minister what arrangement has been made with the contractors for carrying on the work. The original contract specified that they were to be paid so mucfh per yard for excavating the rock.
They get $8.40 per yard for excavating and removing the rock.
I thought the channel had been completed, and that they were simply removing the loose rock.

They are paid $8.40 a yard, which includes blasting, lifting and carrying away the rock.
Mr. .1. D. REID. If the hon. minister looks up the records lie will see that their original contract was to make that channel 14 feet deep. They were paid some $170,000 for going below grade in order to make it 14 feet deep. They have been paid in full for that; but during the past two or three years the government have claimed that owing to the swift water running down between the islands, the loose rock would be carried into this channel, and that it was this loose rock whidh this firm were dredging. But no loose rock can be carried in there, because the dam has been built above and there is still water at that point, so that there is nothing to wash down. If it was worth $8.40 a yard to blast and excavate the rock, why is it worth $8.40 a yard to take out the loose rock ? I doubt if there is any. Last year the government had a Mr. EMMERSON.	,
very nice deal with this firm to pay them $425 per day for the use of the dredge ; but if they are getting $8.40 a yard for removing loose rock, they are doing still better. I venture to say that the Minister of Railways and Canals dare not leave that contract open to competition. If he does, he will get that loose rock excavated for less than $2 a yard. What did the government pay for blasting and dredging rock under the contract of W. A. Allan ? $4.25 a yard. The dam has been placed across ttie islands, so that there is no current there now.

The dam is not completed.
Mr, J. D. REID. It is completed. It was completed last year, so far as not allowing that water to go through is concerned. I walked across that dam last year from one side to the other, and I venture to say that the deputy minister will not say that there is any swift water there. Surely the minister will not offer that as an excuse for paying $8.40 a yard now. If these gentlemen were paid in full for blasting and dredging this out to 17 feet, why are they paid again for the same work ? Why is that necessary ? Their engineer certified to it and they got paid in cash for it.
When were they paid?
They were paid year after year for any work they did of this kind. ' The certificates of the department show it.
During all the years since 1878 ?

Yes, and I will tell you what happened. When the Cornwall canal enlargement came on, these same men took a contract on the canal and got a certificate from the engineers in charge that this channel was perfect, and the government took it off their hands and notified steamboat men that boats drawing 14 feet of water could go safely through, but it turned out that they had not dredged it all out. There were spots where there was only -ten feet of water, but they knew the channel would never be used for the reason that y-ars ago the ex-Minister of Railways decided to have this outside lock, of which we were speaking a few minutes ago, put right at the rapids, so that vessels could lock there and avoid these dangerous rapids. Therefore this dangerous canal was never used. Steamboat men and insurance men knew that this canal was useless ind that they could not use it, even if there were seventeen feet of water in it. But they offered, if the government would experiment by running a steamboat down the channel, drawing fourteen feet of water, ind drawing a tow, to run vessels down. But the government would not assume the responsibility. After my explaining the

matter in the House, I remember well when the steam barge * Niagara ' went down loaded with lumber, and was turned in the channel and went down backwards, and from that day to this there has never been a steamboat run down that channel except some small propeller drawing only a few feet of water. After I showed the House that there was only ten feet of water in the channel and demanded an investigation, the government appointed Mr. Kennedy, engineer of Montreal harbour, to investigate, and he proved that the statement I made in this House was exactly true. He proved that there was only ten feet of water in the channel and in quite a number of spots only nine feet and ten feet, although the contractors had been paid in full for dredging it out to fourteen feet. So we are today jmying these contractors for excavating in what is practically stall water $8.40 a yard, and we are paying them that price for blasting and excavating work which had already been paid for. Is it the present minister who made this agreement, because I cannot believe that any sane man would ever make such a contract, and surely there must be something wrong if he ever did make an agreement of that kind ? Did he really make that agreement himself ?

The work had been going on under agreement before I took charge of the department. Of course I am not shirking any responsibility, but simply answering the question of my hon. friend. The wTork has been carried on under an agreement made and acted upon during the years he has spoken of.
When was the agreement made ?
It was a new agreement made in 1899 or about that time.
It has been made since last session. They were not at work last year.
They did not work last year, but that did not cancel the agreement.
That agreement of $S.40 per yard was completed, and they were working at $425 a day two years ago. Now they have got back to the old agreement of ?8.40 per yard.
The only time 8425 per day was paid was when they were surveying.

I can prove by the Auditor General's Report that they'were paid $42o per day for two or three seasons, and they did not get $425 per day when surveying. I can prove that if necessary. That is a statement reflecting on the ex-Minister of Railways, namely, that they got $425 per day when they were surveying. That is not the fact. They were paid something like 2021
$60 or $70 a day. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals knows that.
This is not the Kennedy matter, as I am informed by my deputy.
Do you mean to say that they received $425 per day for surveying ?
And for removing some loose materials.
Season after season they were paid $425 per day.
The arrangement now is $8.40 per yard. That would be a reasonable price. I know that after competition very recently in Halifax, we awarded a contract at over $9 in that harbour.
What depth of water -about forty or fifty feet ?
About 25 feet.
And this is about ten or eleven feet.
The price was $9 right in the harbour of Halifax where they could have no current and not very much tide, and whatever tide they would have would be an advantage.
There must have been an estimate made of the quantity of rock to be excavated before this was let at $8.40 per yard.
There was no rock to be excavated. The work was done and paid for.
I would like to know what the estimate was based on. There must have been some estimate before this work was ready. What was there to be excavated and how many yards ?

The hon. minister states that this is for blasting and excavating. But long ago that contract was performed. The prism quantities were paid for, and the contractor was paid for taking out this excavation and an extra foot paid for besides. Sometimes he necessarily had to go two or three feet below the prism, but he was paid in full for all the quantities that were in the prism and cuttide of it. What is it he is excavating now that he is being paid for ?

This is the actual excavation to bring it to a proper depth. The work is carried on, as I am advised, under the strict supervision of the officers of the department. Measurements are accurately taken and the payments are made on those measurements at $8.40. It strikes me that $8.40 is reasonable enough. The whole trend of discussion on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite has been to demonstrate that this work has been unnecessary.
It has nothing to do with the necessity of it, but it is a question of work actually done.

But that is the trend of the argument-that it is unnecessary. Here is a work that was determined upon away back about the seventies, or before that, for all I know, and, for year after year, under succeeding governments, it has been carried on to the stage where $75,000 will complete the excavation. It is a question whether it will be advisable to complete the work or whether you will throw away $S78,000, -which Canada has spent upon it, and not attempt to use the channel. It seems to me the part of wisdom to expend the sum I have named to complete the work and utilize the channel.

The minister avoids the question I have put to him. Here is a contract entered into for the purpose of deepening the canal to 14 feet with a certain width. The government paid the full amount for that contract. It was extended to a further depth of one foot. The government paid the full amount for that. Has the depth or the width been increased, ana has a new contract been made ?
It is 300 feet wide.
What was the original width ?
It was originally 200 feet wide.
And it was made deeper. But has not that all been paid for according to the quantities long before this ?
No.
When was the new contract entered into ?
As near as I can discover, it was in 1899 that it was determined to widen it, and the contract -was rene-wed with that view.	.

Notwithstanding the statement of the hon. minister's predecessor in the House, that he would do nothing of the kind-that he would not enter into any new contracts and that he would see to it that expenditure ceased altogether on this work ?
My hon. friend is assuming-
No, I heard the statement, and I will quote it from ' Hansard.'

The question arose as to the 14-foot channel, and the minister said they had the depth and the width that was required. I read the item from the paper showing that some one disputed that, and he asserted most emphatically that the measurements had been carried out and all they were doing was sweeping the bottom of the channel so as to take away the pieces of Mr EMMERSON.
rock or other material that had been carried down by the current in the spring. He said that the width and depth had been gained, and he announced to the world that any vessel not drawing more than 14 feet could pass through that channel.
The minister will find the passage at page 4301 of ' Hansard ' of 1902 :
Somebody must have done it. Surely it was done under the instructions of the engineer.

No. I want to be understood expli-citely by the committee. I stated at the last meeting of the committee when this item was referred to, that the contractor was notified that we were not going to continue the work.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This .vote last year was secured with a view to going on. It was a vote of $75,000. $35,000 of which was estimated to have been expended up to .Tune 30th. To complete the work, as I am informed, clean up the channel and remove all possible obstructions will cost the $40,000 which we are asking for now and $35,000 additional.
Will the hon. minister confine himself to the question I asked ? When was the contract entered into for the purpose of widening this channel ?

As I am advised, the original contract was entered into years ago, and under that contract work has been done year by year, and when the work was not performed, of course, the contract was not in operation, but it was not cancelled. Then, when the work was authorized by a vote of parliament last session, the department went on under that original contract.
Then there was no new contract ?	.
No.
Then the minister was misinformed ?

Is it not a fact that for a couple of seasons after the contract had been taken off the hands of the government, after the work had been completed and the $8.40 a yard contract was finished, the government made another contract with these gentlemen to clear out this channel and paid them by the day ? Instead of paying them $8.40 per yard, they paid them $425 a dav, and in that way they paid them $70.000, $80,000 or $100,000 for work of this kind.	*

I would not like to say what was done. I can furnish a copy of" the contract. My hon. friend is asking me whether there was such a contract. I will get that information. I do not want to make statements that are not in accordance with the very letter of the contract. Therefore, instead of answering my hon.

friend, I will furnish a copy of the contract before the supplementaries are considered.
I do not believe that the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals would ever make that contract on his own responsibility. It may be all right for the minister to put it on the deputy minister.

I have not put it on the deputy. My hon. friend should not make that statement. I have no such thought in my mind. The deputy is not in a position to give me information definitely, and therefore I do not care to make any statements that are not in accord with the very letter of the contract.
This original contract for $8.40 a yard was not made by the deputy minister, it was made by the late Mr. Page.
No contract can be made by the minister without the authority of Council, and the deputy minister would have no power to make one.

I assume that. I do not believe the deputy minister would ever recommend either the $8.40 or the $425 arrangement. If he has done it, it was to satisfy the minister ; because in my opinion this matter is not continued from year to year unless there is some deal in the matter. It is very strange that this was allowed to stand for a couple of years, until last fall when an election was supposed to be coming on, and then this old contract springs up again, and is continued, and will be continued I suppose, until this country does something to stop it.
I suppose my hon. friend's suspicions arise from his familiarity with the Conservative regime during all these years that his friends were in power.
This contract was originally let by the Mackenzie government.
But it was continued by the succeeding government.

It was carried on through the Conservative regime because there had to be a channel cut through those rapids, or else some other means would have had to be adopted by which vessels could pass through. I have asked the minister what is the estimated quantity of excavation for this work under the contract, and what the total cost is to be, and unless we get that information, I shall ask the minister to allow this item to stand until we do get it. otherwise we will have to discuss the matter until he consents to produce it.

Two years ago the minister said this contract was closed and that they would notify the contractor to that effect. I assume that was done. Now if that was all settled, how could it be opend
up again at the pleasure of one side or the other ? The contract was closed. Anything done after that must have been done by some new agreement.

The minister says this is going on under a contract made in 1878, that this is an extension of the contract for the widening of the prism. But he must remember that the contract was virtually terminated by myself. A commissioner, Mr. Kennedy, was appointed for the purpose of finding out whether the contractor had performed the terms of the contract, and he found that the proper quantities had not been taken out. Then the contractor went on and took out the proper quantities. After that contract was finished, the contractor went on for a couple of seasons, not under the original contract at all, but was paid at so much a day for the work that was done. Then the minister comes in and says :
I will inquire whether the facts you state are correct or not. Finally he tells the House: I will tell the contractor that his contract is finished and that he will get no more money upon it. In face of that statement the contract is renewed, the old contract of 1878, without tenders, after its expiry. We do not know what the new contract is. The minister says it is an extension of the contract of 1878, but we do not know how the prism is enlarged, or its depth. We want the actual quantities. He comes here without any information and asks the House for a vote of money for a wholly useless undertalyng. The money that is spent upon this job is uselessly spent. The utility of it was done away with when I put a lock into the rapids for the purpose of enabling vessels to go in and pass the rapids. They use the lock entirely and yet this expenditure goes on from day to day. These men are paid the enormous sum of nearly $500 per day and then they get a contract at $8.60 per yard. Does the" hon. minister say upon the advice of the deputy minister that the contract is enlarged ? I understood him to say that the prism is being widened or deepened. If it is so let us get at the exact facts. How much is the prism widened or deepened and what is the new contract 1 We should know this before a dollar of the vote goes through.
The information which is asked for is such as I have stated. I did not anticipate it would be required. I have stated the price and the quantities I will give to my hon. friend again.
Go on to another item if you cannot give us this information. We want this information before this item passes.
I do not think my hon. friends will be unreasonable.
This is getting to be pretty much of a burlesque on parliament.
This contract was entered into many years ago.
And closed many years ego.
Apparently it was not closed. It was not a contract of which time appeared to be the essence.
The hon. gentleman's predecessor said it was closed two years ago.

No, as read by the hon. member who read it from the record of the House, the Minister of Railways and Canals of that day did not make that statement. I did not understand that to be the meaning.
Mr. SPROULE, Did he not make the statement that he would notify the contractor that the contract was closed, and that he would spend no more money on it ? Was not that the statement that was read here ? That is the statement, as I understood it.

Here is the statement, and I will read it again for the hon. minister :
No, I want to be understood explicitly by the committee. I stated at the last meeting of the committee when this item was referred to, that the contractor was notified that we were not going to continue the work.
What date is that ?

May 6, 1902.
Mr. EMMERSON- It is estimated that there are about 9,000 cubic yards of material to be removed from there, and that under the contract under which they are operating we have paid out during the fiscal year ending 30th June the sum of $35,000.
May I ask the hon. minister if that has been paid out on the basis of the old contract or of the new V

I stated that the estimated payment up to June 30th is $35,000. The work has been going on during the month of June and parliament has provided the money for it. I do not want items to be forced through this committee. I want to furnish all possible information, but I think we should make some progress, and I think I can furnish my hon. friend with copies of the contract itself. When I can tell the committee what the contract is, what the arrangement is under which they are working and for which the department is liable, and for which purpose we are voting the money, it seems to me that I am meeting all the expectations that can be formed of a minister placed in a like situation. I have endeavoured to give that information fully. To me it seems to resolve itself down to this point, that it is a question whether the successive governments of this country, having paid out the sum of monev which they have for this work, shall halt when they are within $75,000 of the goal,
or whether they shall throw entirely away all that has been expended because they feel that the expenditure of $75,000 was not expedient.
When we were at the goal two years ago ?
I am informed that we were not.
There must have been some strange fabrication then or there must be now.
I certainly think, from the statements given to me, that we have not reached the goal, and that it will be necessary to have this money expended in order to finish the work.

The hon. minister made the statement that a certain amount of money was paid out during the last fiscal year. I asked him if it was paid out under the contract made with the Mackenzie government in 1878 or under the new contract at so many dollars per day.
Yes, it was paid out under precisely the same terms as contained in the contract entered into originally with the Mackenzie government.
Are we to understand that the original contract provided for the payment of so many' hundred dollars per day ?
No ; it provided for the payment of $8.40 per cubic yard. Those are the terms upon which the money has been paid out during the last fiscal year.

When the matter was up for discussion in 1902, and when Mr. Blair referred to the item, the statement was made in committee then that there was a new contract, and that the contract was for $425 per day. My hon. friend from Grenville (Mr. Reid) says that we paid for 29S days in that very year, not under the original contract, as my hon. friend has stated, but under the new contract at $425 per day. What I want to know is when the original contract ceased, when the new contract was entered into, and whether the money expended last year was paid under the new contract ?

The money paid during the last fiscal year was paid according to the terms of the original contract entered into in 1878. That is that for the work performed of drilling, blasting and excavation, we paid at the price of $8.40 per cubic yard, and it is upon that basis that the work will be carried on during this year if the vote of $40,000 is provided.

I will ask the hon. minister just to listen to this. He says that he continued the payment under the contract made in 1878. As my hon. friend has drawn attention to it, here are the payments on the

Galops canal, one In 1900-1, 298 days at $425 per day, or $126,654.
My statement had reference to the current year. I have been answering my hon. friend in respect to the year ending 30th June, 1904.

The hon. minister says that he is doing this under the contract made in 1S78, and leads the House to believe that that contract is still continuing. The Minister of Railways stated in answer to Mr. Sproule :
He "was notified before the 1st of July, 1901; and he had no authority whatever, expressed or implied, for continuing the work after that date.
Then this question was asked by Mr. Sproule.
Why should the hon. gentleman now ask for a sum to pay him if he had no author-, ity ?
To which the minister replied :
I must he lacking in the faculty of explaining myself if the hon. gentleman has not understood me. I say that I am not asking for anything more than sufficient to pay the drawback that was due and retained in the department, as is usual in all contracts, for work prior to the 1st of July, 1901.
Then I said :
I understand what the hon. minister says perfectly well. Does he mean to say that the work done in 1901 amounted to $300,000? It was a daily contract, so much per day, and there could be no drawback in paying for anything before 1901, and there was a drawback for work done to the extent of $500,000 in 1902.
What I want to draw the attention of the minister to is the fact that the contract was virtually finished under my regime ;1 I ended the contract. The contractor was not re-employed under the contract of 1878, but he continued the work under an agreement with the department at so much per day. He received his payment per day for a couple of years. Then the minister assured the House that not one cent would be paid this man in 1901. If the contract continued while he was doing the day work surely it was finished when the notice was given by the department of the termination of the contract in 1901. The justification that the department now attempts to make for this payment was that it was under a contract of 1878 which has continued up to the present day.
And the ten per cent had been paid back on the completion of all transactions.

The minister must see that he must give the fullest information to the House especially in reference to the
renewal or extension of the contract which he says he made under the contract of 1878. This money must have been expended for an extension of the prism either in width or depth, and he should tell us to what extent that has been made.
Is it because my hon. friend wishes for a copy of that contract of 1878 that he desires this to stand ?
That was furnished seven or eight ye^rs ago. What I want is a copy of the agreement under which they are paid $425 per day.
Do you wish a copy of the extension of 1899.

If my hon. friend objects to going on with this vote without a copy of this contract I think he is quite entitled to it and I am perfectly willing that the vote should stand. I shall bring down everything that is involved in this.

I would ask why it is that after the statement made by Mr. Biair when Minister of Railways and Canals that all that was asked for in the estimates was

the drawback, there was no appropriation in the estimates for this work at all in 1902-3. If that be true -what is the reason that the department has again taken it up.

I assume this was taken up last year. There was a vote last year with respect to it. The proposed vote this year is for $40,000. The reason I have *taken it up this year is that I think the work should be completed when it will only require $75,000 to do it. I am so advised by the chief engineer of the department.

My hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reidl. who seems to understand this canal pretty well, has stated that this is a useless expenditure. He has stated that the department took the work up again last fall because they thought the general election was coming on.
He was only joking when lie said that.
I atn putting the different things together and sizing them up in my own way.
You are taking it seriously.

Very. It looks serious. In 1,002-3 there was no appropriation because there was no election in sight; but there was an election expected last fall, and an appropriation was put in for this useless work. There was no election last fall, but there is expected to be One this fall, and the idea is to expend $75,000 more on this useless work, all for political effect. That is the whole thing in a nutshell. This is a game of politics. You are spending the people's money for the sole purpose of getting votes.
I suppose that has been done right along-that is the reason all this money was expended in 1878 to 1896, and from 1896 down to the present time-by a parity of reasoning.
Is that serious ?

I want to carry the joke as far as it will go.
Item allowed to stand.
St. Lawrence rivers and canals-reducing shoals west of Cornwall canal, $25,500.

This is a revote. This amount Is to be expended in reducing Shoals or obstructions and doing some necessary excavation. The total expenditure in connection with that up to the 1st of May, 1904, was $457,686.69.
How much will it take to finish the work ?
There is supposed to be about 37,000 cubic yards yet to be done, at an estimated cost of 70 cents.

I have been asked by several marine men if it would not be possible to have what is called Mud Island iShoal at the foot of-Carlton Island, near Kingston, excavated. I think it is composed of mud or loose earth which could easily be removed. I know that one steamer, the 'John C. Howard,' worth $150,000, with a cargo worth $50,000, grounded on this shoal and suffered serious damage. All the large vessels when they go to Kingston have to cross this shoal from the main channel, which is on the American side. This is t'he first opportunity I have had of bringing the matter before the House. It is a very small matter and perhaps the minister could inquire into it and provide for it in the supplementary estimates. From what I have been informed, I judge that the work will not cost more than a couple of thousand dollars. The Americans are putting their channel in splendid shape, and I think the minister might very well provide for this small item, which is really imp ;rtant to make our channel safe.

I will call the attention of the Public Works Department to the matter. The dredging or reduction of shoals in the Department of Railways, and Canals is incidental to the canal expenditure. All dredging not connected with the canals is under the supervision and control of the Department of Public Works. However, I will confer with that department on the subject.
Electric light power plant, Welland canal, $100,000.

The total estimated cost of this plant is $250,000. $100,000 was appropriated last year, and the total expenditure up to the 1st of May was $10,766.88. It was estimated that the balance would be paid before the 1st of July, but it will require $100,000 more. The Welland Canal will be illuminated this season by about 250 arc lights of 2,000 candle power, distributed between Port Dalhousie and Port Ool-borne, a distance of twenty-seven miles. At each of the twenty-five locks there will be electric arc lights, while along the banks of the canal there will be a light every 400 feet. In addition there will be special equipment of arc lights to the piers at the head and foot of the canal. It is expected that the new lighting system will be in operation by July 1st.
Where is your plant located ?
At Decew Falls.
What do you pay for your horse-power ?

The supply of electric energy will be obtained from the Lincoln Light and Power Company, of St. Catharines, the power being generated at

Decew Falls by the Hamilton Cataract Company. The price is $14 per horse-power.
You do all the connections and put in all the motors and plant ?
Yes, tenders were asked for all that material.
How long has the contract to run ?
Ten years, if 1 remember correctly ?
The lighting ?
The power.
They do the lighting themselves. [DOT]
Ten years from when?
It is supposed to take effect the 1st of July this year, when we have the material all completed.
How much do they get a year for it ?
$14 per horse-power. I am giving this information from memory and it will be subject to correction. We simply get the horse-power and all the rest is done by the department.
You can calculate what the cost will be.
25 cents a light is the estimate.
Who looks after the repairing of the lights ?
We will need a man to supervise-an electrical man-it may be possible that this can be done by the superintending engineer.
Is that the intention ?

The matter has been discussed. I thought possibly it might be advisable to employ an electrician to have sole charge. Then the other view occurred that possibly it could be in charge of the superintending engineer.
Who is in charge now ?

The works are being put in under the supervision of Mr. Parks, electrician, of Toronto. He is the consulting expert. The construction is under the direction of the superintending engineer. Mr. Parks is the expert upon whose advice the work is being done.
Are there not several expert electricians living in St. Catharines, right where the work is being done ?
As Mr. Parks is the regular electrician 'of the department all through this section of Canada, I did not think it was necessary to employ an outside man.
I suppose there are several officers assisting him ?
No.
Who is it intended shall do the work after this plant is installed ?
I have no one appointed and have no intention other than that somebody will be employed to attend to that work.
Then it is not intended that the workmen on the canal shall do it ?
If the workmen on the canal can do it and at the same time do their other duties, they will do it.
What is the intention of the government ? Is it intended that they shall or shall not do it ?
The matter has not yet been determined.
Do you intend to use the power for opening and shutting gates and moving bridges ?
Yes.
What is the estimated horse-power that will be required for the whole ?
I have not the information. That was given last year, and the officer who has the matter in hand did not think it necessary to be here.
You are sure you can do it for $250,000 ?
That is Mr. Parks's estimate.
You have only voted $200,000-$100,000 this year and $100,000 last year.
An unprovided balance to complete-it will take $50,000.
If it is to be finished by 1st of July, why does not the hon. gentleman take enough to pay for it ?
When these estimates were made up the work had not proceeded far enough to warrant us in asking for an exact vote. A supplementary vote will be necessary.
How many lights do you require ?

At each of the twenty-five locks there will be six electric arc lights, and along the banks of the canal there will be a light for every 400 feet. In addition there will be a special equipment of arc lights for the head and foot of the canal.
How does this expense compare with what the government have been paying for lighting by gas !
It will cost much more.
I would like a more definite statement. There has been very good lighting by gas lamps-four lamps at each lock, two at either end.

By gas it has cost $10,000, but those who patronized the canal were constantly complaining. The modern method of lighting canals is by electricity, and if we are to have an up to date system we must have the canals lighted in this way. The cost will be more-there is no use in pretending the contrary. But the demands of the trade must be recognized. Those having occasion to use the canal seemed to think that the government should light the canal in this modern fashion.
But the hon. minister has not yet told us what the difference is.
I have given $10,000 as the cost of lighting by gas. The cost of electricity will be not less than $15,000, as estimated by the officials.
Besides the capital expenditure ?
Yes.
Does the hon. gentleman say that complaints have been made by the shipping interests that the locks have not been properly lighted ?

The better lighting enables them to save time in the operation of the gates. While the lighting of the gates by gas was fairly good, it certainly did not meet the requirements of the traffic, and I am informed that the shipping interests almost unanimously demanded the electric light.

I live right there, and I never heard that the locks were not properly lighted, with the four gas lamps at each lock distributed so as to give the best light for opening and closing the gates, i have to come to Ottawa to hear the suggestion that there was any delay or trouble caused by the lighting. I can understand that it may be fashionable to have electric light and, as it is fashionable, it is easy to find some people to say that they want it. Here is a large expenditure of money for the installation of a system and a large annual expenditure to follow. And it replaces a system under which the local gas company, so far as I ever heard, has been giving a satisfactory service. I go along the canal and drive up and down every season, and I have never known one of these gas lamps to be out-wherever you see one you see the four.
It was not lighted along the canal, but only at the locks."
The locks are all along the canal.

There may be quite a distance between them, and vessels had to travel long distances that-were not lighted. The fact that these people wanted these lights and were dissatisfied with the old ones is quite consistent with the fact that they did not stop off at St. Catharines and ask my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) to hear their complaints. He says he has to come to Ottawa to find this out. But, the shipping interests would naturally come to Ottawa and make their grievance known to the Department of Railways and Canals. And they were very insistent in their expression of opinion as to not merely the convenience but the necessity of having this light.	*
Where there are no locks ?

They want a light almost as much where there are no locks as where there are. They have bridges all along the canal. The speed of a vessel along the canal is governed very much by the facility with which it can get through these bridges. With electric power for the bridges the vessel can make very much better time.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that 550 lights is the total, distributing as he has described ?
This season about 550 lights of 2,000 candle power, distributed between Port Dalhousie and Port Colborne, a distance of twenty-seven miles.
The cost with gas is about $10,000, and the cost of electricity for 550 lights at 25 cents per light per night would be between $25,000 and $30,000 ?
That includes the power to swing the bridges and gates.

I am not finding fault with this system of lighting, but trying to get at the difference between the two systems. The minister will pay about $30,000 per annum for electric light, and, besides, lie is to pay $14 per horse-power to work the locks. And he has entered into a contract for ten years from 1st July. These statements, I understand, are correct. The hon. gentleman has entered into a ten years contract. I do not know whether the government have a right to cancel that contract. If they have put in such a provision it would be a step in the right direction, because it is well known that the cost per horse-power for electric energy, in view of the great improvement at Niagara Falls, is certain to be very materially reduced, and it would be unwise for the government to enter into a long contract for ten years without introducing a provision for cancelling the contract if they so desired. Is there such a provision in ' the contract ?
No.

Then the government has been very negligent. You cannot And a municipality in Ontario that will enter into a ten years contract for the supply of electric power in face of the wonderful development of electric energy and the rapid decrease of the cost of such development.
$14 per horse-power is a very low price.

I am not disputing that. But my hon. friend must remember that the development of electric power at this moment, especially in that neighbourhood, is going on very fast, and the cost is being rapidly reduced, and will he reduced much faster.
I doubt if you could get it much lower.

We must judge the future by the immediate past. Electric power companies of Niagara Falls to-day are going around among the different municipalities in western Ontario trying to get them to enter into a contract for a long period of time, because they know that the cost of. furnishing electrical power is certain to be rapidly reduced. It is only the transmission of this power for long distances that seems to be the great difficulty to overcome at this moment.

I can confirm what my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has said in regard to the development of electrical energy at Niagara Falls, and I think the government has been negligent of its duty in failing to put in the contract such a clause as he has referred to. I am astonished to find that it has not been done. I understand that in the neighbourhood of St. Catharines, corporations and municipalities, in making their contracts with this very company, say to them : We won't give you this contract unless we have in it a clause by which we can terminate it. But it appears that the government have not asked the company to consent to such a clause being put in. You will not find any village or town or city, or any municipality in the Niagara district, who will make a contract for more than five years without such a clause in it. Everybody in the neighbourhood knows that electrical energy is going to get cheaper all the time, because the cost of the development of that energy is getting cheaper all the time. It is only in its infancy. It seems to me that the government have been remiss in their duty to the people in failing to put in such a clause providing for cancellation of the contract. I venture to say if the government had such a clause in this contract, in five years from now they would be able to get better terms, they would be able to get their electricity
33 per cent cheaper, perhaps 50 per cent cheaper, than they do now. The company would not have objected to putting such a clause in the contract if it had been insisted on.
My hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lancaster) seems to have changed his base. His first objection was to the use of electricity at all.
I never objected to using electricity if it was a good bargain.

But when the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) gives him another idea then he goes on to elaborate it. Now I venture to make this assertion, that you could not possibly get any electrical company in Canada to furnish this power as cheaply as we are getting it now unless you gave them a term of years. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to get up and make such statements, they are very easily made. But, to seriously consider this as a business proposition ; I know something about these matters and I know that twenty-one years is more likely to be the term asked for before companies will go in and place themselves in a position to furnish power. The ten years we have arranged for is a reasonable period. The price charged is very moderate, and I venture to make the statement that there is not anywhere in Canada a more provident contract entered into in regard to electric light.
Will the hon. minister allow- me to tell him that in the present time in the village of Flesherton there is a contract running at $8 per horse-power for five years.
That would be for a very small quantity.

Then a larger quantity ought to be cheaper. I will say to the hon. minister that if he will look into this matter carefully in the next few days I will guarantee him that he will not repeat the statements he made before taking his seat. I am quite w-illing that the statement which I have made to the committee shall be compared with the minister's statement and jl will leave the people of the country to draw their own conclusions.
Are we to understand that this item is to put in the plant ? Is any of it for power, and do I understand the hon. minister to say that the plant will cost a total of about $200,000 ?
The plant will cost $250,000 to light the whole Welland canal ?
$250,000 will equip the whole Welland canal with electrical plant.
I Mr. BLAIN. I want to draw the hon. minister's attention to the statement that was made when this matter was introduced into the House last year. I want the hon. gentleman's attention.
I am trying to give the hon. gentleman my attention. I do not wish to show any discourtesy to my hon. friend.

This was introduced last year for the first time and the reference to it will be found at page 12,900 of ' Hansard ' as follows :
Welland canal, to provide electric light plant, $44,000.
Is this being done bycontract and has the contract been let ?

It will be done hut the work is not yet commenced. We propose to take in this item $55,000 but we have asked in the supplementary estimates a further sum of $45,000, making the estimated cost of the whole undertaking $100,000, which we believe will furnish a complete electric light plant for the whole canal. This estimate is made on the report of an electrL cal engineer. We expect the work will be done by contract.
Mr. EMMERbuN. Yes, that is all right; that is for the electric lighting part of it, but there is another part, the power to operate the gates and machinery all along the canal. There is $100,000 for electric lighting and $150,000 for all of the other.
Will the hon. gentleman say how much the electric light plant Will cost ?
$250,000 will be required for the electric lighting and power plant. The power plant represents $150,000 and the electric lighting plant represents $100,000, the two representing $250,000.
May I ask the hon. minister when he expects to complete this power and electric lighting plant ?

It was hoped to have it completed by the 1st of July this year, but on account of some delays on the part of the contractors and of disappointment in getting material from some of the manufacturers, delay has occurred. We are urging the work forward as fast as possible.

I am afraid I have not understood the hon. gentleman. I understood the hon. gentleman entered into a contract for ten years at $14 per horse power. Wrill he again explain that ? If the lighting is to cost $100,000 and the government is to 'pay $150,000 for the power plant, where does this contract come in for ten years at $14 per horse-power ?

For the power we get to operate this electric lighting and power plant. We are getting the power from the Lincoln Electric Light Company. We Mr. EMMERSON.
provide all the machinery and plant and we simply take the power from them.
Now, we have it perfectly plain. It is $100,000 for lighting, $150,000 for installing the power plant and you have entered into a contract for furnishing power at $14 per horse-power for ten years.
I stated that the contract was to commence on the 1st July. What I meant was that it was to commence when we require the power.
As soon as you have the plant finished ?
Yes, from the time we take the power.
The hon. minister has given an explanation that seems to be satisfactory. He has made a distinction between the power for working the gates and the lighting.

That distinction was made in the remarks of last year. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance then explain-ted that he would require $100,000 for the electric lighting plant. This year we ask for electric lighting and power plant $200,000 and then there will be $50,000 which we will have to provide for in the supplementary estimates.
That is a further explanation.
I made that explanation some time ago.

My hon. friend has stated that last year the hon. Minister of Finance .made it quite plain that there would be an electric lighting plant and that the electric lighting plant would cost $100,000 which money was voted. Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell us why he puts into this item the electric lighting plant ?
Why not put it in ?

The hon. Minister of Finance last year said that to provide the electric light plant for the Welland canal there would be required $100,000. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals now says that that will complete the electric lighting plant. The $100,000 was voted. Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to tell us why he is now including in this item a sum of money for the electric light plant when it was stated that the $100,000 voted last year would equip the lighting [plant ? The item we have before us reads:
Welland electric lighting and power plant, $100,000.
If the hon. Minister of Finance was correct in his statement last year, and if the money voted last year was put into this

plant, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals should strike out the words ' electric lighting plant,' and say ' power plant, $150,000.' .

No ; the sums merge together. They are interwoven. It is all connected with the Welland canal. Surely we are not going to split hairs at this time of the night.
Mr. BLA1N. We are not splitting hairs. It is my hon. friend who is splitting hairs.
I am not splitting hairs; i am only splitting up the electric lighting from the power.

That statement was made last year, that this estimate was made on the report of an electrical engineer. Are we to understand that when the electrical engineer was instructed to examine the Welland canal preparatory to the installation of an electric lighting plant there was nothing considered about a power plant at all ? I would ask the minister if he would be good enough to give us the two reports of the electrical engineer, the one for the plant for the electric lighting of the canal and the other for the power plant ?
I think these reports wore furnished to the House last year when the matter was discussed, but I shall be very happy to furnish them again.
There will be no mistake about it? The minister will furnish the two reports to which I have referred ?
I think they are both included in one.
And the estimates given by the electrical engineer for the separate works ?
I will give the whole thing.

The minister a fevv moments ago stated that the old system of lighting was insufficient. Has any accident ever occurred from defective lighting on the Welland canal during the long period it has been in operation ?
I am not aware of any.
The hon. minister says that complaints were made ; people mav complain against a thing that is Pt'!" fectly safe, but their complaints may not be well-founded.
Horse cars would have done us, I suppose ; we need not have had electric tramways. They got along at one time with tallow candles.

Does my hon. friend seriously say that at one time there .vere horse cars running on the Welland canal ? The people of Canada want to have the expenditure of their money treated seriously. They do not want a burlesque in this House.
I did not say anything about having horse cars on the Welland canal.
We were talking about the Welland canal.
I was endeavouring to illustrate to my hon. friend the fact that we could get along with gas.
We have got a lot from the minister to-night.
It was better to have tlio electric light, a.ucl the s<uue rule would apply on all the canals. They are using electric lights on canals everywhere.

The only reason which the hon. minister gives for incurring the large increase of expense necessitated by the use of electric lighting on the canal is that the demands of the shipping interests required that there should be electric light ; yet the minister confirms the information I had, that there never has been an accident upon the canal because of defective lighting. ^ Bearing that in mind, I would ask the minis- * ter if there is any other reason for placing this much larger burden on the people of Canada than the one which he gave ?
What number of horsepower have you contracted for ?
I cannot recall the number.
What portion of the year do you require to keep the electric lights going ?
During the season of navigation only, at the termini and at the bridges.
What number of months is navigation usually open ?

From about the 15th of April to about the middle of December,
I think.
Item allowed to stand.
Welland canal-to remove obstructions and make other improvements, $225,000.

There is a revote of $30,000 out of the vote last year of $217,000. The works include the : Deepening of the rock cut at Ramey's Bend : Total estimated cost. $100,000 ; voted for 1903-4, $75,000 ; required for 1904-5, $30,000 revote plus $25,000, in all $55,000. That will finish these works. There is also the removal of the centre piers of three bridges ; Allanburg bridge-estimated cost. $50,000 ; Marlatt s bridge, $50,000 ; bridge 11. the Grand Trunk Railway, Thorold, $70,000 ; in all, $170,000. The total expenditure for removing obstructions up to the 30th of June, 1903,wa* $94,122.98 ; expended from the 30th ot

June, 1903, to the 1st of May, 1901, $97,375.55 ; total amount expended up to the 1st of May, 1904, $191,498.53. The deepening of the rock cut at Ramey's Bend is made necessary by the fact that Lake Erie has been gradually lowering for some years.
It is rising now, isn't it ?
It is just now ; but it has been gradually lowering for some years.
How much lower is it at the present time than the standard level on which the entrance to Port Colborne was based ?

The rock cut is being deepened two feet, giving 17 feet of water at ordinary level of Lake Erie and 15 feet at low water. The work is being done by contract. The contractors are Waddell, Battle & Manley ; the rate per yard is $2.90. The lowest tender was accepted. The water level has dropped as low as 4 feet below what was known as low level.
This excavation is still needed a couple of feet lower ?
Yes, and that is an extreme drop. The averag drop has not been so great. At any stage under these conditions there will be fourteen feet of navigation.
With the present mitre sills in the locks, if the water is lower by 4 feet than was contemplated when the canal was built, then the deepening you propose to do is only 2 feet.

The engineer says that with the rock cut deepened 2 feet there will be 17 feet at ordinary water and 15 feet at low water. Five old centre pier bridges have been removed in the past two years at Ilumberstone, the Junction, Welland, Quaker bridge and Port Robinson : the Allanburg and Marlatt's bridge are the only ones remaining on the summit level, to be removed by the departement. Bridge 11 is a bridge built by the department in 1880 for the Grand Trunk Railway, and is operated by the department. It is very badly located and interferes with navigation. more than any other bridge on the canal.
Does that finish the removal of all the obstructions ?

No, it does not. There is the Niagara street bridge in St. Catharines and several others that have to come under my notice. We are doinsr the work gradually. It is necessary to re move these centre piers in order to give more freedom to the boats.
I suppose when you allow a railroad to build a bridge over a canal and you choose afterwards to have it altered. you do it at your own expense ?

There is a case like that with the Grand Trunk Railway Company at present. We are calling upon them to do that work. We do it with respect to this bridge because the Grand Trunk was there before the canal, that is, the new canal.
In connection with these bridges, are they to be given by contract ?
Yes, altogether.
And the work now being done is being done by contract ?

Yes.
To deepen portions of summit level between Port Colborne and Thorold, $100,000.
What is the total amount required, and the depth ?

The deepening of this portion of the canal'is rendered necessary, in order to maintain 14 feet navigation, bv the gradual lowering of Lake Erie. Two feet is being excavated from the bottom of the canal, giving 17 feet of water at normal level of Lake Erie and 15 at low water. McGann & Finn are the contractors ; rate, 38| cents per cubic yard. The estimated cost is as follows :
Amount expended to 30th June, 1903.. .$125,330
Voted for 1903-1904	loo'ooo
Required for 1903-1904	 ioo'oOO
Unprovided balance to	complete	 124,670
Total	$450,000'
So that that portion of tlie canal, Lake Erie level, is lower than the depth of water on the mitre sill ?
No, it got filled in.
If it was lower than that, you would have to lower the mitre sill also.
They did lower the mitre sill four feet the year before last.

Was there not some talk of doing something at the Niagara river with a view of deepening the water at Buffalo, and would not that have the effect of lowering the water in the Welland canal ? The press of Buffalo is'agitating for some action with the view of preventing the lowering of Lake Erie.

The Americans are
talking that way.
Would not the deepening of the water at Buffalo have some effect in keeping the same depth of water we have now at the Welland canal ?
I have not given the matter very much study, and the opinion I might express might not be of value to the committee.

Y'ou deepen the mitre sill at the lake entrance four feet. Does

this improvement take effect on the reaches at the entrance below the mitre sill ?
They are not a foot lower than the mitre sill. That was lowered.
When do the reaches get to the level of the mitre sill that was lowered ?
When they are two feet below the old mitre sill.
Then the mitre sill of the lock coming into these reaches will be two feet lower than the reaches. What is the object of that ?
When they had to water out, they put it down to that level.

For the purposes of navigation there ought to be an average in the reaches of at least two feet more depth than the mitre sill of the lock. You have lowered the mitre sill of the lock four feet. I want to know what you have deepened the reaches. I understand you have deepened them two feet.
Yes.
Have you lowered the lock at the other end of the reach to the depth to which you have lowered it at the entrance ?
That is being lowered now.

Then you contemplate to lower the whole of these reaches to at least one foot lower than the mitre sill of the lock at some time or other, and the new lock that is lowered you lower to the level of the mitre sill coming out at Lake Erie ?

SYhat is the policy of the government in so far as the deepening of the Welland canal is concerned ? There has been an agitation to have it deepened to 17 feet. At present the government have deepened the entrance at Port Colborne so that a vessel drawing 17 feet of water can come into the entrance of the Welland canal. A vessel, therefore, if the Welland canal had 17 feet navigation, could go through that canal and carry about 100,000 bushels ; but as the depth is only 14 feet, she can only load 60,000 or 65,000 bushels of grain. If you had the extra depth, the vessels could load at Duluth or Port Arthur and proceed to Kingston where they could lighten. The freight rates are higher, of course, on account of the smaller cargoes, and I would like to know if the government have formed any policy in so far as this is concerned ? The public are anxious to know this, more especially as the Americans are contemplating enlarging the- canal from Buffalo to New York. Another matter which I have brought to the attention of the government from year to year is this. Even
though they should undertake to deepen the Welland canal, ae 1 have suggested, it would take five or six years to complete that work, and during all that time we would not enjoy the advantage of the additional depth. ' in so far as getting trade through the St. Lawrence route instead of its going by Buffalo is concerned. I suggested that if the government would take over that small line of railway from Port Colborne to Port Dalhousie and operate it and lighten the vessels at Port Colborne and give them the grain again at Port Dalhousie, they could make it part of the canal system.
The expense of operating this railway would not be very large-not even as great as the interest on the money needed to enlarge the canal. And, by the adoption of my suggestion we would be able to immediately notify the trade that we were prepared virtually to give them the 17-t'oot navigation throughout the canal by lightering at Port Colborne and taking on again at Port Dalhousie. Of course, this was done years ago, and it is done now if the freights are sufficiently large for the vessel to be able to afford it. But, during the greater part of the season of navigation, freight from Port Arthur to Montreal is about three cents a bushel, and, as this railway charges from H cents to 2 cents for lightering, it does not pay the vessel to take that extra quantity of grain off, because they do not make anything out of it. I do not know whether the hon. minister has ever considered this idea. I have brought it up year after year. It may be he can give us some information as to whether there is a chance of the government taking it up, or he may tell us what the policy of the government is in deepening the canal. As the hon. minister knows even the smallest trifle will have its effect in deciding the routing of grain. Even one-sixteenth of a cent per bushel will decide the route. Taking off the canal tolls appeared a small concession, and yet the result was seen in the great increase in the quantity of grain that passed through the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. The suggestion that I make, if carried into effect, I believe, would double the tonnage coming by the St. Lawrence route.

Naturally, I have not had much opportunity to study these questions. But the whole question is under consideration in connection with the proposed improvemets at Port Colborne. Of course. I cannot give my hon. friend any idea of what the ultimate result will be.
Have we at present a 14-foot navigation on the Welland canal ?
Yes, 14 feet on the mitre sills.

One of the locks, by mistake, was put above the level and there is not the 14-foot navigation on the long

stretch from Lake Erie. The minister is deepening it to give the 14-foot depth.

In connection with what the minister said about considering the question-no doubt this matter will be dealt with by the Transportation Commission. Can the minister tell us when we may expect a report from that Commission ?

The Commission is now visiting different points. They have made an interim report with respect to one section of the country, and it is expected that there will be one covering the Port Colborne section, as they recently went there and made a thorough investigation.
Which section have they reported on ?
They have made an interim report with respect to the port of St. John. They started by going to St. John and Halifax.
Was the lowering of the mitre still done by contract or by day labour ?
By day labour.
What was the total cost ?

Between $11,000 and

Welland canal-improvements at Port Colborne entrance, $300,000.
This it an item on which there will be a discussion. We want a full explanation of the scheme.
Then, I think we have gone as far as we can.

Before the committee rises I would ask the minister if he would kindly leave one item on the Trent Valley canal for discussion until Wednesday. I am obliged to be absent on Monday and Tuesday.
Some resolutions reported.
FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved the adjournment of the House.
Will the minister be good enough to tell us what business will be taken up on Monday ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not seen the Prime Minister, but I understood that the intention was to take up Bills on Monday. If there is any change I will see to it that notice is sent to the leader of the opposition. I think several ministers will be absent, and the Minister of Railways will be unable to continue on his estimates. So, the intention is to take up some Bills.
Any Bill in particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The most important is the Militia Bill.
I see that that is to be dropped ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is that dropped ? My bon. friend (Mr. Haggart) may know, but I have not been informed to that effect.
Then, the Militia Bill may come up ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it likely. All Bills on the Order Paper will be open.
